title: Authorization and authentication: chapter 7 of the 3rd edition run through a Bitcoin Script interpreter and checked against the standards and Bitcoin Core's tests

nodes.label: Transaction scripts and the Script language
nodes.body: This branch opens the chapter's central idea. When you receive bitcoins you must decide who has permission to spend them, which the book calls authorization, and every full node must be able to tell the authorized spender from everyone else, which it calls authentication; the instructions and the proof are checked by thousands of independent full nodes that all have to reach the same verdict (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The original description of Bitcoin used a public key for authorization and a signature for authentication, and the version that was released instead gave both jobs to a small programming language called Script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch opens the chapter's central idea. When you receive bitcoins you must decide who has permission to spend them, which the book calls authorization, and every full node must be able to tell the authorized spender from everyone else, which it calls authentication; the instructions and the proof are checked by thousands of independent full nodes that all have to reach the same verdict (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The original description of Bitcoin used a public key for authorization and a signature for authentication, and the version that was released instead gave both jobs to a small programming language called Script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch matters because every other branch of the chapter is a pattern written in this language. A payment to a key hash, a multisignature, a script hash, a timelock, a witness program and a taproot output are all Script, or a rule about where Script is stored; a reader who knows what the language can express, and what it refuses to express, can read each of them as a few lines of a stack machine instead of as a list of unrelated tricks. The book states the consequence in one sentence: transaction validation is not based on a static pattern but on the execution of a scripting language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has two groups. The first, the language and its limits, says what Script is - a Forth-like stack language - and what it is not: it is deliberately not Turing complete, it keeps no state between runs, and the consensus rules cap its size and its work. The second, locking, unlocking and running a script, shows how an output carries a condition, how an input carries the data that meets it, what counts as success, and how the two are run one after the other since a repair in 2010 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked examples run a small stack machine of about thirty lines, written in the standard library, in the reader's own browser.

Two cautions apply to the whole branch. First, the word script is used for several different byte strings in a transaction, and it is only the context - the output being spent, the input spending it, the witness - that says which one is meant. Second, the chapter describes the language as it is used, and some of what it describes is policy rather than consensus: policy is the stricter set of rules a node applies to unconfirmed transactions before it relays them, and consensus is the set every node must apply to the transactions in blocks. Each time a limit appears, the text says which of the two it is (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: The language and its limits
nodes.body: This group describes the language itself before any payment pattern is built from it. Script is a stack-based language in which numbers and other data are pushed onto a stack and operators take their inputs from the top of that stack and put their results back on it. The group covers the stack, the two properties that the book names as the reason the language is safe to run on every node in the world - it cannot loop, and it remembers nothing between runs - and the numeric limits that the consensus rules add (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group describes the language itself before any payment pattern is built from it. Script is a stack-based language in which numbers and other data are pushed onto a stack and operators take their inputs from the top of that stack and put their results back on it. The group covers the stack, the two properties that the book names as the reason the language is safe to run on every node in the world - it cannot loop, and it remembers nothing between runs - and the numeric limits that the consensus rules add (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because the language is run by an adversary-facing machine. Every transaction is validated by every full node, so anyone can send every node a script and make it run; the book therefore treats the missing features as the design. If scripts could loop without bound the validation of one transaction could stall the network, and if scripts could read state from earlier runs two nodes with different histories could disagree about the same transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The five sections go from the inside out: the language and its stack machine, the way a stack makes arithmetic look backward, the absence of loops that makes the language Turing incomplete, the absence of state that makes verification stateless, and the numeric limits - script size, operation count, item size, stack depth and key count - that Bitcoin Core enforces (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Each section ends in an example that the reader can run.

The group describes consensus behaviour, so a rule that is stricter in the relay policy of one release is not a rule of the language. Where this group quotes a limit it is read from the Bitcoin Core source at the commit pinned for the course, and where the book gives a different figure the difference is stated (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: Script
nodes.body: Script is the programming language that the original Bitcoin software introduced for transaction validation. The book describes it as a Forth-like stack-based language, says that both the script placed in an output and the legacy input script used in a spending transaction are written in it, and says that it is a very simple language that requires minimal processing and cannot easily do many of the fancy things modern programming languages can (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example is the book's own first script, 2 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL, which adds two numbers and asks whether the sum is five.

paras.text: Script is the programming language that the original Bitcoin software introduced for transaction validation. The book describes it as a Forth-like stack-based language, says that both the script placed in an output and the legacy input script used in a spending transaction are written in it, and says that it is a very simple language that requires minimal processing and cannot easily do many of the fancy things modern programming languages can (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example is the book's own first script, 2 3 OP_ADD 5 OP_EQUAL, which adds two numbers and asks whether the sum is five.

Script is what makes Bitcoin payments programmable rather than fixed. Most legacy transactions had the form payment to Bob's Bitcoin address and used one script, called pay to public key hash, but scripts can be written to express a vast variety of conditions, and an output that simply asks for the answer to an arithmetic puzzle is as valid to the network as one that asks for a signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Understanding the language is therefore the way to understand every output type in the rest of the chapter.

The reader meets Script wherever a transaction is decoded: an explorer prints the locking script of an output as a line of words such as OP_DUP OP_HASH160 and the unlocking data as hexadecimal, and Bitcoin Core's source defines every word of the language as a numbered opcode in its script header (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The words are written with the prefix OP_, and the book notes that the prefix is sometimes omitted in examples, so that OP_ADD and ADD name the same operator (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A script is a sequence of items processed from left to right. A data item is pushed onto the stack; an operator pops its inputs, computes, and may push a result. The program in the example does this for 2 3 ADD 5 EQUAL: after the two pushes the stack holds 2 and 3, ADD replaces them with 5, the next push adds another 5, and EQUAL replaces the pair with 1 because the two are equal. The program that runs it is a loop over the words of the script that handles about twenty operators, and it is the same machine that the following concepts use.

Bitcoin's real interpreter is much larger than the thirty-line machine used for the examples, and the examples say so each time they simplify. The real language has 113 named opcodes in Bitcoin Core's header, stores every item as a string of bytes, and disables some opcodes outright; the machine in the examples is a teaching model of the same behaviour, while the library written for this course runs the real rules and was checked against 1,237 script tests that ship with Bitcoin Core (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: The script execution stack
nodes.body: A stack is a very simple data structure that the book compares to a stack of cards. It has two base operations: push adds an item on top of the stack and pop removes the top item. The scripting language executes a script by processing each item from left to right; numbers, which the book calls data constants, are pushed, and operators push or pop one or more parameters from the stack, act on them, and might push a result (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A stack is a very simple data structure that the book compares to a stack of cards. It has two base operations: push adds an item on top of the stack and pop removes the top item. The scripting language executes a script by processing each item from left to right; numbers, which the book calls data constants, are pushed, and operators push or pop one or more parameters from the stack, act on them, and might push a result (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The stack explains why Script looks backward to a reader used to ordinary programming. The sum one plus one is written 1 1 OP_ADD because the operator comes after its operands, and the same reversal applies to every condition: the book's flow control puts the test before IF, and a signature check puts the signature and the public key before the operator that checks them. Once the reader sees every operator as a function of the top of the stack, long scripts become short sequences of small steps (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book works one script by hand: 2 7 OP_ADD 3 OP_SUB 1 OP_ADD 7 OP_EQUAL calculates 2 plus 7 minus 3 plus 1 and asks whether the result is 7. The stack grows to two items after each number is pushed and shrinks back to one after each operator, which is the pattern 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1 that the worked example prints for the nine words of the script, and it ends with a single true value. The book invites the reader to try it with pencil and paper (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The operators that compare, such as OP_EQUAL, push true as the number 1 and false as 0, but success is decided differently: a script succeeds when the top item of the stack is true, which is any nonzero value, as the next concepts explain. An operator that finds too few items on the stack does not wait for more; the script fails at that point, which is why the dummy element of the multisignature operator, met in a later branch, has to be present (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 2 7 OP_ADD 3 OP_SUB 1 OP_ADD 7 OP_EQUAL
nodes.definition: A stack is a pile of items with two basic operations, push and pop, and the script engine reads a script from left to right, pushing data and letting each operator pop its inputs and push its result.

nodes.label: Turing incompleteness
nodes.body: Turing completeness is the property of a language that can compute anything a general computer can, which requires loops or recursion. The book says Script has many operators but is deliberately limited in one important way: there are no loops and no complex flow control capabilities other than conditional flow control. That ensures the language is not Turing complete, so scripts have limited complexity and predictable execution times, and Script is not a general-purpose language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Turing completeness is the property of a language that can compute anything a general computer can, which requires loops or recursion. The book says Script has many operators but is deliberately limited in one important way: there are no loops and no complex flow control capabilities other than conditional flow control. That ensures the language is not Turing complete, so scripts have limited complexity and predictable execution times, and Script is not a general-purpose language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The limitation is a defence. The book explains that the language cannot be used to create an infinite loop or another logic bomb embedded in a transaction to mount a denial-of-service attack on the network, and it reminds the reader that every transaction is validated by every full node, so a limited language prevents transaction validation from being used as a vulnerability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The work a script can demand is bounded by its length and by the number of operations it is allowed to contain, both of which a node can read before it runs anything.

Without a repeat operator, a repetition has to be written out. The example doubles the number 1 ten times by writing DUP ADD ten times: the script has 21 words and leaves 1,024 on the stack, and doubling twenty times would need 41 words, so the script's size grows with the work it asks for. Bitcoin Core adds a second bound: it counts the operations that are not simple number pushes and fails a script that has more than 201 of them, and it fails any script longer than 10,000 bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Conditionals exist - IF, ELSE and ENDIF - but they only choose between written-out branches.

Incomplete is not the same as weak. Because scripts cannot loop, the useful patterns of the chapter - signatures, hash locks, timelocks, thresholds, trees of alternatives - are all expressed as a few comparisons, and richer computation is done by the parties off chain, with only a commitment and its proof placed on chain. The book returns to this when it describes taproot, where the whole contract may never appear on chain at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: no loop construct: ten repetitions cost twenty words
nodes.definition: Script is deliberately not Turing complete: it has no loops and no flow control but conditionals, so every script ends and its running time is predictable.

nodes.label: Stateless verification
nodes.body: A language is stateless when nothing outside the program and its inputs can change what the program does. The book says the Bitcoin transaction script language is stateless: there is no state prior to the execution of the script and no state saved after it, and all the information needed to execute a script is contained within the script and the transaction executing the script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A language is stateless when nothing outside the program and its inputs can change what the program does. The book says the Bitcoin transaction script language is stateless: there is no state prior to the execution of the script and no state saved after it, and all the information needed to execute a script is contained within the script and the transaction executing the script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Statelessness is what lets thousands of independent computers agree. The book states the conclusion: a script will predictably execute the same way on any system, so if your system verified a script you can be sure that every other system in the network will also verify it, which means a valid transaction is valid for everyone and everyone knows this. That predictability of outcomes is described as an essential benefit of the Bitcoin system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In practice the inputs of a script run are few and explicit: the two scripts, the data stack passed between them, the transaction that contains the input and the amount and locking script of the output it spends. Nothing else - no clock, no random number, no database - is read, which is why the timelock opcodes of a later branch do not ask the clock but compare their argument with fields of the spending transaction. The example runs the book's first script five times and obtains one distinct result.

Statelessness describes the script engine, not the whole of validation. Whether an output is still unspent depends on the state of the network, namely the set of unspent outputs, and a node checks that separately before it runs any script; that check is the job of the ownership record described in the chapter on transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the same script gives the same result on every machine
nodes.definition: Script verification is stateless: there is no state before a script runs and none saved afterward, so a script runs the same way on any system.

nodes.label: Consensus limits of a script
nodes.body: A limit of a script is a number that the consensus rules fix in advance so that no script can demand unbounded work or memory. The source of Bitcoin Core declares them as named constants: a script may be at most 10,000 bytes long, may contain at most 201 operations that are not number pushes, may push items of at most 520 bytes, may hold at most 1,000 values on its stack, and may check at most 20 public keys in one multisignature operator (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: A limit of a script is a number that the consensus rules fix in advance so that no script can demand unbounded work or memory. The source of Bitcoin Core declares them as named constants: a script may be at most 10,000 bytes long, may contain at most 201 operations that are not number pushes, may push items of at most 520 bytes, may hold at most 1,000 values on its stack, and may check at most 20 public keys in one multisignature operator (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

These constants turn the idea of predictable execution into numbers. With 1,000 items of at most 520 bytes the stack cannot hold more than 520,000 bytes, which is what the worked example multiplies out, and with 201 operations the running time is bounded as well. The book states the first limit when it discusses alternatives to conditionals: legacy script is limited to 10,000 bytes, which practically limits a script to a few hundred conditional branches at most (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The engine checks each limit while it runs. It refuses a script longer than the size limit before running a byte, counts operations as it reads them, rejects a push larger than the item limit, and fails with a named error - script size, operation count, push size or stack size - when a bound is crossed; the multisignature operator adds the number of keys it checks to the operation count (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Tapscript, met in the last branch, lifts two of them: its scripts are not limited to 10,000 bytes and not limited to 201 operations, and a per-script budget of signature checks takes the place of the operation count (Wuille et al., 2020).

The limits are consensus rules for ordinary scripts but several related numbers are policy only: a standard bare multisignature output may list at most three keys, a standard witness script is at most 3,600 bytes, and a standard input script at most 1,650 bytes, so a transaction can be valid in a block yet refused by relay nodes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A reader who builds a script near a limit should test it against the relay policy as well as the consensus limit.

nodes.label: Locking and running a script
nodes.body: This group follows a single spend from the two halves of its condition to its verdict. An output script states the condition under which the output can be spent, an input script supplies data that meets it, and the node runs them to decide whether the input is a valid authorization. The group also covers what the verdict means and the vulnerability that led the original design to be changed in 2010 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group follows a single spend from the two halves of its condition to its verdict. An output script states the condition under which the output can be spent, an input script supplies data that meets it, and the node runs them to decide whether the input is a valid authorization. The group also covers what the verdict means and the vulnerability that led the original design to be changed in 2010 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The split is the core of authorization and authentication in Bitcoin: the sender of a payment writes the condition into the output, and the receiver proves much later, when spending, that the condition is met. Because the proof is checked only when it is used, the same machinery supports a one-key payment, a multisignature, a timelock and a contract, and the sender needs to know nothing about how the receiver will satisfy the condition (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The five sections take the pieces in order: the output script, the input script, the rule that a script succeeds when it leaves a true value on top of the stack, the separate execution of the two scripts with the stack passed between them, and the +1 OP_RETURN+ bug that the separate execution repaired. The worked examples use real bytes from mainnet transactions for the scripts and the small stack machine for the control flow.

The words locking script and unlocking script are used in older material for the output script and the input script, and the owner's earlier course notes use them; the third edition prefers output script and input script, and so does this chapter. Segregated witness adds a third place where unlocking data can live, the witness, which the segwit branch treats (Altunel, 2021) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Output script
nodes.body: An output script is the part of a transaction output that holds the locking condition. The book defines it as the script that specifies the conditions that must be met to spend the output in the future, such as who is authorized to spend the output and how they will be authenticated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example is the most common legacy script, a payment to a public key hash: 25 bytes that begin with the operator DUP, byte 118, and end with the signature operator CHECKSIG, byte 172, around a 20-byte hash.

paras.text: An output script is the part of a transaction output that holds the locking condition. The book defines it as the script that specifies the conditions that must be met to spend the output in the future, such as who is authorized to spend the output and how they will be authenticated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example is the most common legacy script, a payment to a public key hash: 25 bytes that begin with the operator DUP, byte 118, and end with the signature operator CHECKSIG, byte 172, around a 20-byte hash.

The output script is where the sender decides what the receiver must prove. The sender writes it once, when creating the output; it then sits in every full node's set of unspent outputs until somebody spends the output, so its size is paid for by every node for as long as the output exists. That cost is the reason the chapter's later patterns - hash of a script, witness program, taproot key - all try to make the output script short (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader sees an output script in the vout list of any decoded transaction, where an explorer prints it both as bytes and as words, and in Bitcoin Core's solver, which recognises the standard templates by comparing a script with their shapes: pay to public key, pay to public key hash, pay to script hash, bare multisignature, data carrier and the witness programs (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Alice's output in the chapter on transactions, and the landmark transactions of this chapter, are all read this way.

A node validating a spend copies the output script of the referenced output and runs it after the input script. The book stresses that all of this is done on copies: the original data in the previous output and in the input is never changed, so the previous output is unaffected by failed attempts to spend it, and only a valid transaction makes the output count as spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every input of a transaction is checked independently against the output it names.

nodes.example: OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG
nodes.definition: An output script, called scriptPubKey in the code, states the conditions that must be met to spend the output in the future, such as who is authorized to spend it and how they will be authenticated.

nodes.label: Input script
nodes.body: An input script is the part of a transaction input that supplies the data meeting an output script's condition. The book describes it as a script that satisfies the conditions placed in an output script and allows the output to be spent, present in every transaction input; most of the time in legacy transactions it contains a digital signature produced by the user's wallet from the private key, but not all input scripts must contain signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example is the input script of the first input of the pizza transaction of 2010, which holds two items: a 73-byte signature and a 65-byte public key.

paras.text: An input script is the part of a transaction input that supplies the data meeting an output script's condition. The book describes it as a script that satisfies the conditions placed in an output script and allows the output to be spent, present in every transaction input; most of the time in legacy transactions it contains a digital signature produced by the user's wallet from the private key, but not all input scripts must contain signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example is the input script of the first input of the pizza transaction of 2010, which holds two items: a 73-byte signature and a 65-byte public key.

The input script is the proof half of authorization and authentication. The output script says who may spend; the input script is where the spender shows they are that person, by producing a signature that only the holder of the private key can make. Because the proof is created at spending time, the holder can keep the private key offline until then, and because it is only data, the same input script format serves every condition from one signature to a complicated tree of alternatives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In a decoded legacy transaction the input script appears as scriptSig, in hexadecimal and in words, and in a segwit transaction it is empty and the proof sits in the witness instead. Bitcoin Core refuses to relay a standard input script longer than 1,650 bytes, and a consensus flag introduced with pay to script hash requires the input script of such a spend to contain only data pushes (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A node reads the input script as a list of pushes: each item is a length byte followed by that many bytes of data, and the engine places the items on the stack in order, so that the last item pushed is on top. The output script is then run on the same stack; the signature and key lie where the output script's operators expect to find them. This is why the order in the example matters: the signature first, the public key on top, matching the order in which the P2PKH script consumes them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The input script of a legacy transaction is part of what the signature hash covers in a different way from the rest of the transaction, and it is also the part that third parties could change without invalidating the signature, which made the transaction identifier malleable before segregated witness. That story belongs to the chapter on transactions and to the witness group of this one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: <signature> <public key>
nodes.definition: An input script, called scriptSig in the code, is a script that satisfies the conditions placed in an output script and so allows the output to be spent; in legacy transactions it usually holds a signature and a public key.

nodes.label: When a script succeeds
nodes.body: A script succeeds when two things hold: it ran to the end without an error and the top value on the stack is true. The book puts it as a tip: transactions are valid if the top result on the stack is TRUE, which is any nonzero value, and invalid if the top value is FALSE, meaning the value zero or an empty stack, if execution was halted explicitly by an operator such as VERIFY or OP_RETURN, or if the script was not semantically valid, such as an OP_IF that was not terminated by an OP_ENDIF (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A script succeeds when two things hold: it ran to the end without an error and the top value on the stack is true. The book puts it as a tip: transactions are valid if the top result on the stack is TRUE, which is any nonzero value, and invalid if the top value is FALSE, meaning the value zero or an empty stack, if execution was halted explicitly by an operator such as VERIFY or OP_RETURN, or if the script was not semantically valid, such as an OP_IF that was not terminated by an OP_ENDIF (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This rule is the single place where all of the chapter's conditions turn into a yes or a no. A signature operator, an equality test, a timelock check and a hash comparison all end by leaving a value on the stack or by stopping the script, and the verdict is read only from the top of the stack afterwards. A designer who understands this reads any script by asking what it leaves on top, and what makes it stop.

Bitcoin Core's function that decides truth, CastToBool, returns false for an item made only of zero bytes and also for the byte string that is zero with its sign bit set, the so-called negative zero, 0x80; any other item is true. After both scripts have run, the engine fails with the error EVAL_FALSE if the stack is empty or its top item is false (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The example prints the verdict for five items: the empty item, 00 and 80 are false, while 01 and the two-byte item 0001 are true.

Truth in Script is about the item, not about the number: a value of 0x00 0x00 is false, and so is 0x80, even though the two have different bytes, whereas 0x00 0x01 is true. The standard relay policy adds a stricter requirement, called the clean stack rule, that exactly one item remains and that it is true; the consensus rule asks only that the top item be true (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: the top item is true: any non-zero value
nodes.definition: A script succeeds when it runs without error and leaves a non-zero value on top of the stack; zero, negative zero, an empty item and an empty stack are false.

nodes.label: Separate execution of the two scripts
nodes.body: In the original Bitcoin client the output and input scripts were joined and executed in sequence as one script. For security reasons this was changed in 2010, because of a vulnerability known as the +1 OP_RETURN+ bug, and in the current implementation the scripts are executed separately with the stack transferred between the two executions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book spells out the order: first the input script is executed using the stack execution engine; if it runs without errors and has no operations left over, the stack is copied and the output script is executed on that copy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: In the original Bitcoin client the output and input scripts were joined and executed in sequence as one script. For security reasons this was changed in 2010, because of a vulnerability known as the +1 OP_RETURN+ bug, and in the current implementation the scripts are executed separately with the stack transferred between the two executions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book spells out the order: first the input script is executed using the stack execution engine; if it runs without errors and has no operations left over, the stack is copied and the output script is executed on that copy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The separation limits what an unlocking script can do. An input script can only put data on the stack; it cannot run to a premature end of the whole check, because its execution is complete before the locking script starts. The Bitcoin Core function that verifies a spend carries a comment that records the reason, saying that the two scripts must be evaluated sequentially on the same stack rather than being simply concatenated, with a reference to CVE-2010-5141 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The example performs the book's arithmetic both ways. Written as one script, 2 3 ADD 5 EQUAL leaves the value 1. Run as an input script 2, which leaves the stack holding the number 2, and then as an output script 3 ADD 5 EQUAL on that stack, it leaves the same value: the stack is the interface between the two, and for ordinary scripts the result is identical. The difference appears only for operators that stop a script, which is the subject of the next concept (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The words if it runs without errors and has no operations left over deserve care. The check for a valid ending is applied to the final stack after both scripts have run; the input script itself may leave any number of items. Pay to script hash and segregated witness later add a third and a fourth stage to this sequence, copying the stack again and running a script that was revealed by the input; those are separate concepts of later branches (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: the input script runs first; its stack is passed to the output script
nodes.definition: Since 2010 the input script and the output script are executed one after the other, with the stack that the first leaves transferred to the second, instead of being joined into a single script.

nodes.label: The +1 OP_RETURN+ bug
nodes.body: The +1 OP_RETURN+ bug is a vulnerability of the first Bitcoin software that let anyone spend any output. In version 0.3.0 the node joined the input script, a code separator and the output script into one script, and its OP_RETURN operator simply set the program counter to the end of the script, which ended the run with whatever was on the stack. An input script consisting of the number 1 followed by OP_RETURN therefore ended the whole check with a true value on top, and the output script, whatever it demanded, never ran (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Nakamoto, 2010) (Nakamoto, 2010).

paras.text: The +1 OP_RETURN+ bug is a vulnerability of the first Bitcoin software that let anyone spend any output. In version 0.3.0 the node joined the input script, a code separator and the output script into one script, and its OP_RETURN operator simply set the program counter to the end of the script, which ended the run with whatever was on the stack. An input script consisting of the number 1 followed by OP_RETURN therefore ended the whole check with a true value on top, and the output script, whatever it demanded, never ran (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Nakamoto, 2010) (Nakamoto, 2010).

The bug is the reason the chapter says scripts are executed separately. The Bitcoin Wiki's list of vulnerabilities records it as CVE-2010-5141, dated 28 July 2010, affecting wxBitcoin and bitcoind, with the effect that OP_RETURN could be used to spend any output, rated as theft and easy to exploit (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). In version 0.3.7 the source verifies the input script and the output script with two separate runs, and OP_RETURN returns false, which is the behaviour that all later software keeps (Nakamoto, 2010) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP342 describes the same flaw in its own words: in versions up to and including 0.3.5 the original OP_RETURN terminated script execution immediately and returned pass or fail from the top stack element, which permitted unconditional theft by a third party who placed an OP_RETURN in the input script (Wuille et al., 2020).

The worked example is a model of the two designs on a lock that asks for the preimage of a hash. In the old design an attacker's input script 1 RETURN stops the combined script with a true value on the stack, so the check passes; in the new design the same input script fails at once, and only an input script that pushes the secret satisfies the lock. The example shows the outcomes (True, False, True): old design accepts the thief, new design refuses the thief, new design accepts the owner.

The word return is misleading, because in current software OP_RETURN does not return a value; it makes the script fail. The same opcode is used on purpose in the next branches to make an output provably unspendable, which is possible only because the script engine now treats it as an error. The book's data-recording section builds on that (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: CVE-2010-5141: an input script of 1 OP_RETURN spent any output
nodes.definition: In the first release the two scripts were joined and OP_RETURN jumped to the end of the joined script, so an input script that began with a true value and then executed OP_RETURN made any output spendable by anyone.

nodes.label: Locking to a key
nodes.body: This branch follows the oldest and still the commonest way of controlling an output: locking it to a key. The original description of Bitcoin put the public key itself in the output, and the authentication came from the receiver in the form of a signature that committed to the spending transaction; the released software made the mechanism more flexible, and the book then describes the form that dominated legacy transactions, the pay to public key hash script, whose output holds only a hash of the key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The branch also explains what the signature operator checks, because every later branch ends in it.

paras.text: This branch follows the oldest and still the commonest way of controlling an output: locking it to a key. The original description of Bitcoin put the public key itself in the output, and the authentication came from the receiver in the form of a signature that committed to the spending transaction; the released software made the mechanism more flexible, and the book then describes the form that dominated legacy transactions, the pay to public key hash script, whose output holds only a hash of the key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The branch also explains what the signature operator checks, because every later branch ends in it.

The branch matters because a signature is the proof that ends almost every script in the chapter. A reader who knows exactly what a signature covers - which bytes of the spending transaction are hashed, which hash type was chosen, how the signature is encoded - can read multisignatures, timelocked contracts, witness programs and taproot spends as variations on one act of authentication, and can see why each later upgrade changed the way the hash is computed.

The branch has two groups. The first, from a public key to its hash, follows the output script from the bare key of 2009, through the 20-byte hash that a legacy address encodes, to the script that checks both the hash and the signature. The second, checking a signature, opens the signature operator: the message that is signed, the choices a signer has about what to commit to, and the byte format of the signature itself. The worked examples verify, in the browser, the signature of the first payment between people.

The chapter on signatures that follows this one explains the mathematics of ECDSA and schnorr signatures; this branch stays at the level of the script that calls them, and where it needs a number from the mathematics - the order of the curve, the size of a signature - it states the number and says where it comes from (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: From a public key to its hash
nodes.body: This group covers the three ways an output has been locked to a single key. The earliest is the pay to public key script, in which the output holds the key. The second ingredient is the public key hash, the short digest of a key that a legacy address encodes. The third is the pay to public key hash script, which puts the digest in the output and asks the spender to reveal the key and sign with it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers the three ways an output has been locked to a single key. The earliest is the pay to public key script, in which the output holds the key. The second ingredient is the public key hash, the short digest of a key that a legacy address encodes. The third is the pay to public key hash script, which puts the digest in the output and asks the spender to reveal the key and sign with it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The sequence is a history of trade-offs between size, privacy and convenience. The bare key is the simplest script but the output is as long as the key and the key is public from the moment the output exists; the hash is shorter and hides the key until the output is spent, and it lets an address be a short string that a person can copy; and the script that checks the hash and then the signature gives the receiver the same proof of ownership the bare key gave.

The three sections each end in a worked example on real bytes: the 67-byte script of the first payment between people, the address that the 20-byte hash of the generator point encodes, and the input of the pizza payment of 2010, which is run step by step through the script. The census of block 775,072 gives the proportions in today's traffic (mempool.space, 2026).

The word address names the Base58Check or bech32 string that encodes a hash, not a script; a wallet turns the address back into the script before it builds the output. A reader who sees the script in an explorer is therefore looking one step closer to what the nodes actually check than a reader who sees the address.

nodes.label: Pay to public key
nodes.body: A pay to public key output, written P2PK, is the form the first description of Bitcoin used. The book says the original description used a public key for authorization: Alice paid Bob by putting his public key in the output of a transaction, and Bob authenticated himself with a signature that committed to a spending transaction, such as one from Bob to Carol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script is the public key followed by the signature operator, and it is spent by an input script consisting of a single signature.

paras.text: A pay to public key output, written P2PK, is the form the first description of Bitcoin used. The book says the original description used a public key for authorization: Alice paid Bob by putting his public key in the output of a transaction, and Bob authenticated himself with a signature that committed to a spending transaction, such as one from Bob to Carol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script is the public key followed by the signature operator, and it is spent by an input script consisting of a single signature.

P2PK matters as the base case: it shows authorization and authentication in their purest form, one key and one signature, with no hash in between. The first payment between people, in block 170 on 12 January 2009, spent an output of this kind and created two more: its input is a 71-byte signature, and its outputs of 10 and 40 bitcoins are locked with 67-byte scripts (mempool.space, 2026). Every other single-key script in the chapter is this one with some indirection.

The reader meets P2PK in the oldest blocks, in the coinbase outputs of the first years, and wherever a script is built by hand; Bitcoin Core's script solver still recognises it as one of its standard templates, the pay to public key type, and the book names it in the introduction of the chapter (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example reads the locking script of the output that the block 170 transaction spends: 67 bytes, beginning with the byte 65 that pushes a 65-byte uncompressed public key and ending with byte 172, the signature operator.

The public key sits in the output from the moment the output is created, so it is visible in every full node's set of unspent outputs and in the blockchain for as long as the output is unspent. The hash form described next keeps the key out of view until the spender reveals it. The 65 bytes of an uncompressed key are also longer than the 33 bytes of a compressed one, which is why later outputs use compressed keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: <public key> OP_CHECKSIG
nodes.definition: A pay to public key output holds the public key itself followed by the signature operator, so that it is spent by a signature that the key can verify; it is the form in which Bitcoin was first described and used.

nodes.label: Public key hash
nodes.body: A public key hash is a short commitment to a public key. The book describes the construction in its P2SH section for a script and the same two hash functions are used for a key: the data is hashed first with SHA256 and then with RIPEMD-160, producing a 20-byte hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book states what the hash is used for in a P2PKH script: the Key Hash is the data that would be encoded into a legacy base58check address, and most applications show it in hexadecimal rather than as an address that begins with a 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example encodes the hash of the compressed generator point of the curve, 751e76e8..., with a version byte of 0 and obtains the address 1BgGZ9tc...

paras.text: A public key hash is a short commitment to a public key. The book describes the construction in its P2SH section for a script and the same two hash functions are used for a key: the data is hashed first with SHA256 and then with RIPEMD-160, producing a 20-byte hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book states what the hash is used for in a P2PKH script: the Key Hash is the data that would be encoded into a legacy base58check address, and most applications show it in hexadecimal rather than as an address that begins with a 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The example encodes the hash of the compressed generator point of the curve, 751e76e8..., with a version byte of 0 and obtains the address 1BgGZ9tc...

The hash makes the output shorter and the key private for a while. A compressed key takes 33 bytes and a hash 20; more importantly, an output that holds only the hash reveals nothing about the key until it is spent, and a person can share an address that is a short string of characters with a checksum rather than a long hexadecimal key. The book's chapter on keys describes the address and the compression of keys in detail (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The operator OP_HASH160 performs the two steps in one: it pops an item, applies SHA-256 and then RIPEMD-160, and pushes the 20-byte result. Bitcoin Core's own function for it is named Hash160 and does the same (Bitcoin Core, 2026). RIPEMD-160 is not available in the Python of a web browser, so the example is given the hash rather than computing it; the chapter's library, which includes a RIPEMD-160 written in pure Python that was checked against the C implementation on 131 inputs, computes it in the checks.

A key has two serializations, compressed and uncompressed, and the two have different hashes and therefore different addresses; funds sent to the hash of the uncompressed form can be spent only by presenting the uncompressed key. The book makes the point for segregated witness: a P2WPKH output must be built from the hash of a compressed key, and an output built from an uncompressed key may be unspendable (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: HASH160 of the public key: RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(key))
nodes.definition: A public key hash is the 20-byte digest obtained by applying SHA-256 and then RIPEMD-160 to a public key; the legacy address that begins with a 1 is its Base58Check encoding.

A = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58check(version, payload):              # Base58Check: version byte + payload + 4 checksum bytes, written in base 58
    d = bytes([version]) + payload
    d += hashlib.sha256(hashlib.sha256(d).digest()).digest()[:4]
    n, s = int.from_bytes(d, 'big'), ''
    while n: n, r = divmod(n, 58); s = A[r] + s
    return '1' * (len(d) - len(d.lstrip(b'\0'))) + s
h = bytes.fromhex('751e76e8199196d454941c45d1b3a323f1433bd6')       # HASH160 of the compressed generator point
result = b58check(0, h)", g), g['result'])[1])({})

nodes.label: Pay to public key hash
nodes.body: A pay to public key hash output, P2PKH, is the legacy output that most transactions used. The book defines it as a script that uses an output script containing a hash that commits to a public key, best known as the basis for a legacy Bitcoin address, spent by presenting a public key that matches the hash commitment and a digital signature created by the corresponding private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The output script is OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <Key Hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG, which is 25 bytes: three operators, a 20-byte push, and two more operators.

The book defines it as a script that uses an output script containing a hash that commits to a public key, best known as the basis for a legacy Bitcoin address, spent by presenting a public key that matches the hash commitment and a digital signature created by the corresponding private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The output script is OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <Key Hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG, which is 25 bytes: three operators, a 20-byte push, and two more operators.

P2PKH is the pattern behind the first decade of Bitcoin payments, and it still appears: in the first 599 transactions of block 775,072 there are 194 inputs that spend a P2PKH output out of 1,022 inputs in all, against 626 that spend the segwit equivalent (mempool.space, 2026). It combines two proofs in one output - that the spender has the key the sender had in mind, by the hash, and that the spender controls it, by the signature - and it does so with an output that is 25 bytes, not the 67 of the bare key.

The book gives the input script as <Signature> <Public Key>, and the combined script as <Sig> <Pubkey> OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <Hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG, and walks through the execution in its figures 7-3 and 7-4 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The pizza payment of 22 May 2010 is a real example: its first input spends a P2PKH output with a 73-byte signature and a 65-byte public key (mempool.space, 2026).

The trace has seven steps. The two pushes of the input script leave the signature and the key on the stack; DUP copies the key; HASH160 replaces the copy with its 20-byte hash; the output script pushes the committed hash; EQUALVERIFY compares the two hashes and stops the script with a failure if they differ; and CHECKSIG consumes the signature and the remaining key and leaves true if the signature is valid for the spending transaction. The stack holds 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 2 and 1 items after the seven steps, and the library confirms that the real input is accepted and that the hash of the key in it equals the hash in the output.

The result is true only if both halves hold. A correct key with a forged signature fails at CHECKSIG, and a valid signature made with a different key fails at EQUALVERIFY, because the hash does not match. The most common wallet error with this script is the compressed or uncompressed choice: the script commits to the hash of exactly one serialization of the key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: A pay to public key hash output script contains a hash that commits to a public key, and it is spent by presenting a public key that matches the hash together with a signature made by the corresponding private key.

nodes.label: Checking a signature
nodes.body: This group opens the signature operator. Three questions come in order: what the operator does when it runs, what exactly the signature is a signature of, and how the signature is written down as bytes. The first is the subject of OP_CHECKSIG, the second of the signature hash and its hash types, the third of the DER encoding of an ECDSA signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group opens the signature operator. Three questions come in order: what the operator does when it runs, what exactly the signature is a signature of, and how the signature is written down as bytes. The first is the subject of OP_CHECKSIG, the second of the signature hash and its hash types, the third of the DER encoding of an ECDSA signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The questions matter because everything a transaction promises is only as strong as the commitment inside its signatures. The book frames the point: in Bitcoin's use of digital signatures the message being signed is the transaction, or more accurately a hash of a specific subset of the data in the transaction, called the commitment hash, so the choice of subset decides what a signer can later be held to, and what a third party may still change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The three sections are in the order the engine meets them. OP_CHECKSIG pops a public key and a signature, strips the hash type from the end of the signature, builds the commitment hash for the transaction and the script being run, and verifies. The signature hash section describes how the hash depends on the hash type, and the encoding section describes the bytes. The first payment between people is verified end to end by a standard-library program in the page.

The mathematics of the signature, and the signing algorithms of ECDSA and schnorr, belong to the next chapter; the group quotes it only for the numbers a script reader needs. The commitment hash is computed in three different ways in Bitcoin - the legacy algorithm, the version 0 witness algorithm of BIP143 and the taproot algorithm of BIP341 - and this group describes the legacy one, leaving the others to the witness and taproot branches (Lau et al., 2016) (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: OP_CHECKSIG
nodes.body: OP_CHECKSIG is the operator that turns a signature into an answer. The book describes the verification algorithm it relies on: it takes the message, a hash of parts of the transaction and related data, the signer's public key and the signature, and returns true if the signature is valid for this message and public key; verification means that only the controller of the private key that generated this public key could have produced this signature on this transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). As a script operator it pops the public key from the top of the stack, then the signature, and pushes 1 or 0.

paras.text: OP_CHECKSIG is the operator that turns a signature into an answer. The book describes the verification algorithm it relies on: it takes the message, a hash of parts of the transaction and related data, the signer's public key and the signature, and returns true if the signature is valid for this message and public key; verification means that only the controller of the private key that generated this public key could have produced this signature on this transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). As a script operator it pops the public key from the top of the stack, then the signature, and pushes 1 or 0.

OP_CHECKSIG is the authentication step of almost every pattern in the chapter: the P2PKH script, the pay to public key script, the witness program for a key hash, the keys inside a multisignature, the single key of a taproot spend. It is also the expensive operator, which is why the consensus rules count signature operations and why tapscript replaces the operation count with a budget that is spent on each signature (Wuille et al., 2020).

The last byte of the signature is the hash type; the engine removes it, builds the commitment hash for the transaction, the input being checked and the script being run, and verifies the remaining DER signature with the public key. The example does this for the block 170 payment in standard-library Python: it takes the transaction, replaces the input script with the locking script of the output being spent, appends the hash type as four bytes, hashes the result twice with SHA-256, and verifies the signature against the 65-byte key in the locking script. It prints True for the real message and False for a message that differs by one, and runs in about 0.04 seconds.

A failing signature does not by itself stop the script; the operator pushes false and the script continues, which is why the standard relay policy added the NULLFAIL rule that a failing signature must be empty, so that nobody can change a failing signature without invalidating the transaction. Bitcoin Core reports the error SIG_NULLFAIL for it. In tapscript the rule is part of consensus: a non-empty signature that does not verify fails the script at once (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.example: <signature> <public key> OP_CHECKSIG
nodes.definition: OP_CHECKSIG pops a public key and a signature, checks the signature against a hash of the spending transaction, and pushes true if it is valid and false otherwise.

nodes.label: The signature hash and its hash types
nodes.body: The signature hash is the message that a Bitcoin signature actually signs. The book explains that a signature proves a commitment by the signer to specific transaction data, in the simplest form to almost the entire transaction, and that a SIGHASH flag, a single byte appended to the signature, says which part of a transaction's data is included in the hash signed by the private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). There are three flags - ALL (0x01), NONE (0x02) and SINGLE (0x03) - and a modifier ANYONECANPAY (0x80) that combines with each by bitwise OR, giving six values.

paras.text: The signature hash is the message that a Bitcoin signature actually signs. The book explains that a signature proves a commitment by the signer to specific transaction data, in the simplest form to almost the entire transaction, and that a SIGHASH flag, a single byte appended to the signature, says which part of a transaction's data is included in the hash signed by the private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). There are three flags - ALL (0x01), NONE (0x02) and SINGLE (0x03) - and a modifier ANYONECANPAY (0x80) that combines with each by bitwise OR, giving six values.

The hash types are what make partially built transactions possible. ALL, the default, commits to every input and output and is what simple wallets use. With ALL|ANYONECANPAY several people can each add an input to a transaction whose outputs are fixed, the book's crowdfunding construction; NONE gives a blank check, since anyone may write the outputs; NONE|ANYONECANPAY gives a dust collector. Because the flag itself is part of the hashed data, a miner cannot change it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

To compute the legacy signature hash the signer makes a copy of the transaction, blanks the input scripts of the other inputs, puts the locking script of the output being spent in the input being signed, omits or truncates fields according to the flag, serializes the result, appends the flag as four bytes and hashes the whole with SHA-256 twice. The book describes the same steps in words; Bitcoin Core's 500 test vectors for it all reproduce with the chapter's library (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The legacy algorithm has a flaw that its successors repair: with SINGLE, if the input has no output with the same index, Bitcoin Core's code returns the constant 1 as the hash, so the signature signs nothing about the transaction. BIP143 keeps the behaviour but commits zero instead of one in the equivalent case, and BIP341 refuses to sign at all. The book also lists the BIP118 proposal for new flags, which is not part of Bitcoin's rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lau et al., 2016).

nodes.example: SIGHASH_ALL = 0x01 commits to all inputs and all outputs
nodes.definition: The signature hash, or commitment hash, is the digest of a modified copy of the transaction plus the hash type, and the hash type, one byte appended to the signature, says which parts of the transaction the signature commits to.

nodes.label: Signature encoding (DER)
nodes.body: An ECDSA signature is two numbers, r and s, and the way they are written as bytes is a rule of the protocol. The book says that for ECDSA the encoding uses an international standard called the Distinguished Encoding Rules, DER, while for schnorr signatures a simpler serialization is used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The bytes are: 0x30, the length of what follows, 0x02, the length of r, r, 0x02, the length of s and s; Bitcoin appends one more byte, the hash type. The input script of the block 170 payment holds exactly such a push: 70 bytes of DER and the hash type 1.

paras.text: An ECDSA signature is two numbers, r and s, and the way they are written as bytes is a rule of the protocol. The book says that for ECDSA the encoding uses an international standard called the Distinguished Encoding Rules, DER, while for schnorr signatures a simpler serialization is used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The bytes are: 0x30, the length of what follows, 0x02, the length of r, r, 0x02, the length of s and s; Bitcoin appends one more byte, the hash type. The input script of the block 170 payment holds exactly such a push: 70 bytes of DER and the hash type 1.

The encoding matters because a signature that can be written in more than one way is a malleable signature. Before BIP66, the OpenSSL library that Bitcoin used accepted some encodings that were not strict DER, and a third party could rewrite a valid signature into another valid form and change the transaction identifier. BIP66 made strict DER a consensus rule; Bitcoin Core's chain parameters record that it applies from height 363,725, and the repair is also visible in the standard relay policy, which adds the rule that the number s be at most half the order of the curve (Wuille, 2015) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Lau et al., 2016).

A parser reads the sequence in order and rejects anything unexpected. The example prints the first byte 0x30, the length 68 of the content, the length 32 of r, the length 32 of s and the hash-type byte 1 for the real signature. The low-S rule rests on a property of ECDSA stated by BIP146: taking the negative of s modulo the curve order gives another valid signature, so a signature with the larger of the two values can be trivially replaced by one with the smaller (Lau et al., 2016).

BIP146, which proposed LOW_S and NULLFAIL as consensus rules, has the status Closed; the rules are nevertheless in force as standardness rules, because Bitcoin Core's standard verification flags include LOW_S and NULLFAIL, so a transaction that breaks them is valid in a block but is not relayed. Taproot signatures are not DER: a BIP340 signature is 64 bytes with an optional 65th byte for the hash type (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.example: 30 <len> 02 <len r> r 02 <len s> s <hash type>
nodes.definition: An ECDSA signature is the pair of integers r and s written in DER, the Distinguished Encoding Rules, followed by one hash-type byte; Bitcoin requires the strict form of DER and policy requires the lower of the two possible values of s.

nodes.label: Scripted multisignatures
nodes.body: This branch is about the first way Bitcoin lets several people share control of one output. A multisignature script lists k public keys and states how many of them, t, must sign before the output can be spent; the book calls this a t-of-k multisignature and gives a 2-of-3 as its example, three listed keys of which at least two must be used to sign (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The branch has two groups: the form of the script with its limits, and an oddity in the way the opcode that checks the signatures reads the stack.

paras.text: This branch is about the first way Bitcoin lets several people share control of one output. A multisignature script lists k public keys and states how many of them, t, must sign before the output can be spent; the book calls this a t-of-k multisignature and gives a 2-of-3 as its example, three listed keys of which at least two must be used to sign (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The branch has two groups: the form of the script with its limits, and an oddity in the way the opcode that checks the signatures reads the stack.

Shared control is the reason the pattern exists and the reason it is the model for several later chapters of the story. A business can require two of three officers to approve a payment, a person can keep one key at home and one in a safe and a third with a trusted service, and two parties who do not trust each other can ask a third to judge a dispute; the author of the proposal that standardized the pattern, BIP11, gave exactly this last case, a three-party escrow with a buyer, a seller and an agent, as its example (Andresen, 2011).

A reader meets multisignatures in wallets that take several signers and in services that keep coins for others. The block of 775,072 used for this chapter's census holds 67 inputs of this kind among its 1,022 inputs: 10 spend a legacy script hash output and 57 spend a witness script hash output, all of them hidden behind the hash forms of the next branches (mempool.space, 2026). Almost nobody locks coins directly with a bare multisignature script any more, but the script inside the hash is the same.

The branch follows a single script from its general form to the details of the machine that runs it. The form is t, then the k public keys, then k, then the opcode OP_CHECKMULTISIG; the input script supplies the signatures; the limits say how large k may be under policy and under consensus; and the oddity and the signature count describe what the engine does when it runs. Every example in the branch is run by the chapter's library, which accepts the same scripts that Bitcoin Core's own script tests accept (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.label: The t-of-k script and its limits
nodes.body: This group states what a multisignature output script looks like and how large it may be. The script is written t, the keys, k, OP_CHECKMULTISIG, where t is the threshold of signatures that must be valid and k is the number of keys listed; the input script that satisfies it holds the signatures, in the same order as the keys they belong to (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group states what a multisignature output script looks like and how large it may be. The script is written t, the keys, k, OP_CHECKMULTISIG, where t is the threshold of signatures that must be valid and k is the number of keys listed; the input script that satisfies it holds the signatures, in the same order as the keys they belong to (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The two sections matter together because a script that is valid in form can still be too large or not standard. A person who builds a 16-key script discovers that it cannot be put in a script hash output, and a person who builds a bare 4-key script discovers that nodes will not relay it; the limits are what turn the general idea into what a wallet may really create.

The first section gives the form and runs a 2-of-3 example with real signatures; the second collects the limits, which are three different numbers for three different places: three keys for a bare script under relay policy, fifteen for a script hash by the size of a script element, and twenty by consensus for every other script. Each number is read from the book and from the source code of Bitcoin Core and then recomputed.

Policy and consensus differ throughout the group. A rule of the relay policy decides which transactions a node passes on, and a miner may still include a transaction that breaks it; a consensus rule decides whether a block is valid at all. The group says each time which of the two a limit is.

nodes.label: Scripted multisignature
nodes.body: A scripted multisignature is an output script that sets a condition where k public keys are recorded in the script and at least t of them must provide signatures to spend the funds. The book calls this t-of-k and notes that earlier editions, and much other documentation, write m-of-n, which is hard to say aloud because m and n sound alike (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The general output script is t, then the k keys, then k, then OP_CHECKMULTISIG, and a 2-of-3 looks like 2 followed by three public keys, then 3 and the opcode; the input script is two signatures, or any other combination of two signatures from the three keys.

paras.text: A scripted multisignature is an output script that sets a condition where k public keys are recorded in the script and at least t of them must provide signatures to spend the funds. The book calls this t-of-k and notes that earlier editions, and much other documentation, write m-of-n, which is hard to say aloud because m and n sound alike (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The general output script is t, then the k keys, then k, then OP_CHECKMULTISIG, and a 2-of-3 looks like 2 followed by three public keys, then 3 and the opcode; the input script is two signatures, or any other combination of two signatures from the three keys.

The pattern turns one key into a group decision. The signatures are independent proofs that two different holders agreed to one transaction, so no single holder can spend alone and the loss of a single key does not lose the funds. BIP11 made the form a standard transaction in 2011 and described the use that motivated it, a three-party escrow in which the buyer sends coins into a 2-of-3 output, the seller fulfils the deal and the agent decides only if the other two disagree (Andresen, 2011).

On the real chain the bare form is rare; in block 775,072 not one of the 1,022 inputs spends a bare multisignature output, while 10 inputs reveal a 2-of-3 script inside a script hash and 41 reveal one inside a witness script hash, as do 5 2-of-2 scripts and a few others (mempool.space, 2026). Bitcoin Core's script solver still treats the bare form as one of its standard templates and reads t and k from it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The example in this section builds the 2-of-3 with the chapter's library, signs with the second and third keys and runs the engine.

The engine reads the combined script from left to right: it pushes the signatures, the number 2, the three keys and the number 3, and then OP_CHECKMULTISIG pops k, the keys, t and the signatures and tests them. It takes the key and the signature that are on top of the stack, tries them together, and moves to the next key whatever happens; a signature that fits is used up, and the opcode succeeds when all t signatures have been used (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Because the signatures are used up in order, they must appear in the input script in the same order as their keys appear in the output script. The example in the page checks signatures by the second and third key against the list in order and then in the reverse order, and the second attempt fails.

The order of the signatures is the trap. Two valid signatures given in the wrong order fail with the engine's EVAL_FALSE error even though each is valid on its own, because the engine never goes back to an earlier key. The input script of a real multisignature spend also needs the extra first element described in the next section; without it the script fails, and the signatures alone are not an input script.

nodes.example: 2 <sig B> <sig C> ... OP_CHECKMULTISIG
nodes.definition: A scripted multisignature output lists k public keys and requires at least t valid signatures from them, given in the same order as the keys, before it can be spent.

nodes.label: Multisignature limits
nodes.body: The limits on the number of keys come from three different places. The book says that Bitcoin Core's relay policy limits multisignature output scripts to at most three listed keys, from 1-of-1 to 3-of-3; that this applies only to bare multisignature scripts and not to scripts wrapped in a P2SH, P2WSH or P2TR structure; that a P2SH multisignature is limited by both policy and consensus to 15 keys; and that all other scripts are limited by consensus to 20 keys per OP_CHECKMULTISIG or OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY, although one script may contain several such opcodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The limits on the number of keys come from three different places. The book says that Bitcoin Core's relay policy limits multisignature output scripts to at most three listed keys, from 1-of-1 to 3-of-3; that this applies only to bare multisignature scripts and not to scripts wrapped in a P2SH, P2WSH or P2TR structure; that a P2SH multisignature is limited by both policy and consensus to 15 keys; and that all other scripts are limited by consensus to 20 keys per OP_CHECKMULTISIG or OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY, although one script may contain several such opcodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The limits explain choices that look arbitrary. A 15-of-15 is the biggest standard script hash multisignature, and the reason is a size, not a design choice: the script is redeemed by pushing it as one element, and a script element may be at most 520 bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Fifteen compressed keys with their length bytes and the three other bytes make 513 bytes; sixteen make 547 and no longer fit. A comment in Bitcoin Core's policy code does the same arithmetic and rounds the largest signature script of a standard input to 1,650 bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The three-key rule is in Bitcoin Core's function IsStandard, which refuses a bare multisignature output whose n is less than one or more than three, and the twenty-key rule is the constant MAX_PUBKEYS_PER_MULTISIG in the script header; the 3,600-byte limit of a standard witness script is in the policy header (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In tapscript, the script language of taproot, OP_CHECKMULTISIG does not exist at all: the engine fails a script that uses it, and the threshold is built with a counting opcode instead, the subject of a later branch (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The example computes the size of a multisignature script from its parts: one byte for the threshold, 34 bytes per compressed key (a length byte and 33 bytes of key), one byte for k and one for the opcode, which is 34 times k plus 3. For 15 keys this is 513 bytes and for 16 it is 547, so the second is more than the 520-byte limit. The library confirms the sums with real scripts and also builds a 15-of-15 script hash and spends it, so that the largest standard case is not only computed but run.

The word limit hides three different rules. Policy numbers can change from release to release, and the book itself says to check IsStandard to see what is accepted; the 520-byte element size and the 20-key count are consensus rules that cannot be changed without a soft fork. A multisignature that is large because it uses 20 keys has to be placed in a witness script hash, where the element limit of 520 bytes does not apply to the witness script.
