nodes.label: The multisig extra-element bug
nodes.body: This group covers two consequences of the way OP_CHECKMULTISIG is implemented. The first is an extra stack item that the opcode pops and ignores, which every multisignature input script must therefore provide; the second is the number of signature checks the opcode makes, which can be much larger than the number of signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers two consequences of the way OP_CHECKMULTISIG is implemented. The first is an extra stack item that the opcode pops and ignores, which every multisignature input script must therefore provide; the second is the number of signature checks the opcode makes, which can be much larger than the number of signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Both matter to people who build scripts and wallets. The extra item is the reason every multisignature input starts with an empty push, and a script that leaves it out fails; the signature count matters because a node's work and a block's allowance are measured in signature checks. A wallet developer who knew neither would build transactions that nodes reject or that cost more than needed.

The first section describes the extra element and how it became a consensus rule, BIP147; the second counts the checks with the real engine for a 1-of-5 spend and shows the book's explanation of why the extra element might have been put there. The book does not decide whether it was a bug or a plan, and neither does this group.

A rule that exists to repair an old oddity cannot be removed afterwards: the book says that the extra element must now be replicated forever. New designs avoid the issue altogether, which is the reason the taproot script language replaced the opcode with a different one.

nodes.label: The CHECKMULTISIG dummy element
nodes.body: The dummy stack element is the extra item that OP_CHECKMULTISIG removes from the stack. The book explains that the opcode should consume t plus k plus 2 items, namely k, the k keys, t and the t signatures, but because of an oddity in the implementation it pops one more, which it ignores when it checks the signatures and which therefore can be anything. It must exist, because an empty stack at that point causes a stack error and the script fails (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The dummy stack element is the extra item that OP_CHECKMULTISIG removes from the stack. The book explains that the opcode should consume t plus k plus 2 items, namely k, the k keys, t and the t signatures, but because of an oddity in the implementation it pops one more, which it ignores when it checks the signatures and which therefore can be anything. It must exist, because an empty stack at that point causes a stack error and the script fails (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The element matters because it is the first thing every multisignature input script contains and because it was once a malleability problem. The book says it became custom to use OP_0, which later became a relay policy rule and eventually a consensus rule through BIP147. The BIP explains the danger: a relay node could change the ignored value without invalidating the script, and for a transaction without witness data this changes the transaction identifier and invalidates children that spend the unconfirmed output (Lau, 2016).

The rule is in the engine itself. Bitcoin Core's comment in the opcode says that a bug causes OP_CHECKMULTISIG to consume one extra argument whose contents were not checked in any way, and that the flag NULLDUMMY verifies it to be of zero length before it is removed; the same flag is in the standard flags of the relay policy (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). In block 775,072 every one of the 91 inputs whose witness script is a multisignature, 57 direct and 34 inside a nested script hash, begins with an empty element (mempool.space, 2026). BIP11 already mentioned the bug in 2011, and BIP147 was deployed together with segregated witness, which activated at block 481,824 (Andresen, 2011) (Lau, 2016) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The engine pops k first, then the k keys, then t, and then the t signatures; the extra element is the next item on the stack. The example in the page pops the items of the book's script in that order and shows that the opcode has taken 7 items and not yet reached the dummy at the bottom of the stack, so that there is exactly one item left for it to pop. The library runs the real thing: a 2-of-3 spend with an empty first element succeeds, one whose first element is the byte 1 fails with the engine's error SIG_NULLDUMMY, and the same spend without the NULLDUMMY flag succeeds, which is how it was before the rule.

The book's formulation that the dummy is something to put in front of the signatures is true but not the whole truth: it is an empty byte array that is pushed by OP_0, and since BIP147 any other value makes the script fail at once. In a segregated witness input, the dummy is the first item of the witness stack and the rule applies there too.

nodes.label: Signature check count
nodes.body: The signature check count is the number of signature verifications an OP_CHECKMULTISIG performs. The book explains that verifying t-of-k signatures can require many more than t or k checks, and gives a 1-of-5 as its example: one signature is compared with the keys one after another until it meets its own, so five checks are done for one signature. The opcode does not know which signature belongs to which key and has to try (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The signature check count is the number of signature verifications an OP_CHECKMULTISIG performs. The book explains that verifying t-of-k signatures can require many more than t or k checks, and gives a 1-of-5 as its example: one signature is compared with the keys one after another until it meets its own, so five checks are done for one signature. The opcode does not know which signature belongs to which key and has to try (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The count is a cost, and it is limited because signature checks are the expensive part of validating a transaction. Bitcoin Core counts them in the function GetSigOpCount, in which an OP_CHECKMULTISIG counts as the number of keys when it directly follows a small number and as 20, the maximum, when the count is not known, and the consensus limit of a block is a sigop cost of 80,000 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP11 recalled the older limit of 20,000 signature operations a block and the consequence that old software counted each multisignature as 20, so that at most 1,000 multisignature transactions fitted in one (Andresen, 2011).

The book offers a theory about the origin of the oddity in the previous section: the original developer might have added the extra element so that a later soft fork could pass a map telling the opcode which signature belongs to which key, which would reduce the work to exactly t checks. That feature was never implemented, and the book says that BIP147 makes it impossible to add in the future (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same count is the reason why tapscript replaced the opcode, in a later branch.

The example uses a model: keys are labels, and the opcode takes the key on top of the stack first, the last key listed, then the next one below. The signature of the last key, k4, is found at the first try, and that of the first key, k0, only at the fifth. The library runs the real engine with a counter around the ECDSA verification: a 1-of-5 spend signed by the last key makes 1 check, one signed by the first key makes 5, and a 3-of-3 makes 3.

The book describes the search as starting with the first key listed; in Bitcoin Core's code the engine starts with the key at the top of the stack, which is the last one listed, and the number of checks in the worst case is the same. A signature that does not match any remaining key makes the whole operation fail early, as soon as more signatures are left than keys, so a wrong signature is not paid for with all the checks.

nodes.example: a 1-of-5 spend by the first key costs five checks
nodes.definition: The opcode compares signatures with keys one by one, and a signature that matches a key that is far from the top of the stack is found only after many failed attempts, so that the number of checks can be as large as the number of keys.

nodes.label: Pay to script hash
nodes.body: This branch is about the output type that lets a payer lock coins to the fingerprint of a script instead of to the script itself. The book says that pay to script hash, P2SH, was introduced in 2012 as a powerful new type of operation that greatly simplifies the use of complex scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script is revealed only when the coins are spent, together with the data that satisfies it, and the network checks both that the script matches the fingerprint and that it succeeds.

paras.text: This branch is about the output type that lets a payer lock coins to the fingerprint of a script instead of to the script itself. The book says that pay to script hash, P2SH, was introduced in 2012 as a powerful new type of operation that greatly simplifies the use of complex scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script is revealed only when the coins are spent, together with the data that satisfies it, and the network checks both that the script matches the fingerprint and that it succeeds.

The branch matters because almost everything that came after it uses the same idea. A script hash output is the first example of a commitment: the payer commits to something without knowing it, the owner reveals it later, and everyone can check the match. The segregated witness outputs of a later branch, and the merkle trees of the taproot branch, repeat the pattern. BIP16 states its aim in one sentence: to move the responsibility for supplying the conditions to redeem a transaction from the sender of the funds to the redeemer (Andresen, 2012).

A reader meets it as a legacy address that begins with a 3. In the saved block of 775,072 there are 139 inputs that spend such outputs, about 14 percent of the 1,022 inputs of its first 599 transactions: 10 reveal a 2-of-3 multisignature script, 95 reveal a nested witness key hash and 34 a nested witness script hash, so that the form is today mostly a wrapper for the upgrades of the next branches (mempool.space, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The first, the mechanism, explains the output script that holds the hash, the redeem script that is presented at spending time, and the address that lets any wallet pay to it. The second, the consequences, lists what P2SH gives its users and the rules that nodes apply to it. All the scripts in it are run by the chapter's library on real signatures, and the hash-and-address steps are checked against the values in the book.

nodes.label: Hashing the script
nodes.body: This group describes how a script becomes a hash and how the hash becomes an address and then a script again. The output script is OP_HASH160, the 20-byte hash of the script, and OP_EQUAL; the input script ends with the script itself, the redeem script, and the data it needs; the address is the Base58Check encoding of the hash with a version byte of 5 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2011).

paras.text: This group describes how a script becomes a hash and how the hash becomes an address and then a script again. The output script is OP_HASH160, the 20-byte hash of the script, and OP_EQUAL; the input script ends with the script itself, the redeem script, and the data it needs; the address is the Base58Check encoding of the hash with a version byte of 5 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2011).

The three parts divide the work between the people involved. The payer needs only the address and a standard output script; the receiver keeps the redeem script and its keys; the node checks the two together. Because each party sees only what it needs, a payer with an ordinary wallet can fund an arbitrarily complicated script.

The first section shows the shape of the output script and the two-stage check of the spend, the second the redeem script and what it must satisfy, and the third the address and its first character. The examples reuse the book's own numbers, the hash 54c557e0... of Mohammed's script and the address 39RF6JqA... that the book derives from it, and recompute them.

The hash does not tell anyone what the script is. A wallet that has lost the redeem script cannot spend a script hash output even if it still has every key, because the script is the thing the hash commits to. Backups of such wallets must keep the script, not only the keys.

nodes.label: Pay to script hash output
nodes.body: A pay to script hash output replaces a long script with a commitment, the digest of a cryptographic hash. The book states the idea in simple terms: P2SH means pay to a script matching this hash, a script that will be presented later when this output is spent. The hash is made by applying SHA-256 and then RIPEMD-160 to the script, exactly as for a public key, so that it is 20 bytes however long the script is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP16 defines the output script as OP_HASH160, then the push-20-bytes opcode with exactly 20 bytes, then OP_EQUAL (Andresen, 2012).

paras.text: A pay to script hash output replaces a long script with a commitment, the digest of a cryptographic hash. The book states the idea in simple terms: P2SH means pay to a script matching this hash, a script that will be presented later when this output is spent. The hash is made by applying SHA-256 and then RIPEMD-160 to the script, exactly as for a public key, so that it is 20 bytes however long the script is (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP16 defines the output script as OP_HASH160, then the push-20-bytes opcode with exactly 20 bytes, then OP_EQUAL (Andresen, 2012).

The output exists to solve the problem the book illustrates with an importer in Dubai. Mohammed's company wants every customer payment locked by a 2-of-5 multisignature of himself, his three partners and their attorney. Without P2SH every customer would have to be given the long script and would need wallet software that builds custom scripts, the resulting transaction would be much bigger and its fee would be paid by the customer, and every full node would keep the long script in the set of unspent outputs until it was spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). With P2SH the customer pays to a short hash.

The output is 23 bytes on the chain: a byte 169 for OP_HASH160, a byte 20 to push the hash, the hash and a byte 135 for OP_EQUAL. The example builds the output script of Mohammed's company from the book's hash and shows that it is 23 bytes whatever the script behind it; Bitcoin Core's function IsPayToScriptHash recognises exactly this shape of 23 bytes, and its solver lists it as the type scripthash (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The spend is checked in two stages. First the input script is run and the redeem script, which is the last item it pushes, is checked against the output script, that is, its hash must equal the hash in the output. Then, if the match holds, the redeem script is taken off the stack and run on what remains, which is the data it needs, such as signatures. The book writes the first stage as the redeem script followed by OP_HASH160, the hash and OP_EQUAL, and the second as the signatures followed by the contents of the redeem script. The library runs both stages on a real 2-of-3 spend, and also with a one-byte redeem script.

The second stage does not exist for old software. A node from before 2012 sees only OP_HASH160, a hash and OP_EQUAL, and accepts any input script that pushes a script with the right hash, whether or not the script then succeeds. The library shows the same thing by running the spend of a redeem script that is always false with the P2SH rule switched off, which is accepted, and with the rule on, which fails. That is why the rule had to be activated by a majority of miners, a story the page tells later.

nodes.definition: A pay to script hash output script holds only the 20-byte HASH160 of a script, so that whoever spends it must present a script that hashes to the same value and then satisfy that script.

nodes.label: Redeem script
nodes.body: The redeem script is the script that a pay to script hash output stands for. The book says it is called that because it is presented to the system at redemption time rather than as an output script. In the book's tables the output script is the hash form, the redeem script is the long multisignature, and the input script is the signatures followed by the redeem script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The redeem script is the script that a pay to script hash output stands for. The book says it is called that because it is presented to the system at redemption time rather than as an output script. In the book's tables the output script is the hash form, the redeem script is the long multisignature, and the input script is the signatures followed by the redeem script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The redeem script moves cost and complexity from the payer to the owner. The book lists the effects: the burden of storage moves from the output, which is kept by every node in the set of unspent outputs, to the input, which is only stored in the chain; it moves from the present, when the payment is made, to the future, when the output is spent; and the fees of the long script move from the sender to the recipient, who must include the redeem script to spend (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets a redeem script as the last push of a legacy input script of an output that starts with a 3. The example parses the input script of a 1-of-2 multisignature spend produced by the library: it starts with an empty push, the dummy of the previous branch, then a signature, and the last push is a redeem script of 71 bytes that ends with the byte 174, OP_CHECKMULTISIG. Bitcoin Core's function that recognises the spend reads the last pushed item as the redeem script in the same way when it counts signature operations (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Because the redeem script is a push, the engine needs no new opcode to read it: after the first stage it takes the last item of the saved stack, turns it into a script and runs it on the remaining stack. BIP16 says exactly this: the serialized script is popped off the initial stack, and the transaction is validated again using the popped stack and the deserialized script as the scriptPubKey (Andresen, 2012). In Bitcoin Core the code that does it is in VerifyScript, directly after the first run (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The redeem script must be kept. Whoever pays to a script hash output cannot tell whether the script behind the hash is valid or can ever be satisfied, so the book warns that a P2SH output is accepted even if the redeem script is invalid, and that an output can be created that cannot be spent later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The 520-byte limit on a pushed item also applies to the redeem script, which is the reason a legacy multisignature stops at 15 keys.

nodes.example: <sig> ... <redeem script>
nodes.definition: The redeem script is the script whose hash is committed to in a pay to script hash output; it is revealed as the last item of the input script when the output is spent and is then executed with the items that precede it.

nodes.label: P2SH address
nodes.body: A P2SH address is a way to write a script hash so that a person can copy it and a wallet can pay to it. The book says that P2SH addresses are Base58Check encodings of the 20-byte hash of a script, just like ordinary addresses are Base58Check encodings of the 20-byte hash of a public key, and that they use the version prefix 5, which results in addresses that start with a 3. The format was defined in BIP13 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2011).

paras.text: A P2SH address is a way to write a script hash so that a person can copy it and a wallet can pay to it. The book says that P2SH addresses are Base58Check encodings of the 20-byte hash of a script, just like ordinary addresses are Base58Check encodings of the 20-byte hash of a public key, and that they use the version prefix 5, which results in addresses that start with a 3. The format was defined in BIP13 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2011).

The address is what makes P2SH usable. The book's example turns Mohammed's script into the address 39RF6JqABiHdYHkfChV6USGMe6Nsr66Gzw and observes that he can now give it to customers, who can use almost any wallet for a simple payment as to any other address; the 3 hints that it is special but otherwise it works in the same way. BIP16 gives the same reason: a fixed-length hash that is short enough to scan from a QR code or to copy and paste (Andresen, 2012).

The example recomputes the book's address from its hash. It writes the version byte 5, the 20 bytes and the first four bytes of a double SHA-256 as a checksum, and encodes all 25 bytes in base 58, which gives 39RF6JqABiHdYHkfChV6USGMe6Nsr66Gzw, the address printed in the book. The library recomputes it in the checks and decodes two other addresses of the book, which belong to the nested forms of a later branch. The testnet version of the address uses a version byte of 196 and begins with a 2 (Andresen, 2011).

The Base58Check steps are those of chapter 4 of the book: a version byte, the payload, a four-byte checksum taken from the double SHA-256 of both, and base 58. BIP13 writes it as the one-byte version, the 20-byte hash and the 4-byte checksum, and chose the version byte so that, after encoding, the leading character is consistent (Andresen, 2011) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The address of a script hash and the address of a key hash differ only in the version byte, and so a typing error is caught by the checksum in the same way.

The address does not say what the script is, and a wallet cannot tell from the address whether the owner can spend it. The BIP13 text also admits that its address is not backward compatible: an old implementation reports the address as invalid and refuses to create a transaction, which is a failure that is safe. Segregated witness later changed the encoding to bech32 for its native outputs, but the nested forms keep the 3 form (Wuille et al., 2017) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: version byte 5 gives an address that starts with 3
nodes.definition: A P2SH address is the Base58Check encoding of the 20-byte script hash with a version byte of 5, which makes it begin with the character 3.

nodes.label: What the hash changes
nodes.body: This group draws together what P2SH changes for the people and the nodes that use it. For people, it is the four benefits the book lists; for nodes, it is a short set of rules about what an input script may contain, how a redeem script is judged and how many signature checks it may hide (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2012).

paras.text: This group draws together what P2SH changes for the people and the nodes that use it. For people, it is the four benefits the book lists; for nodes, it is a short set of rules about what an input script may contain, how a redeem script is judged and how many signature checks it may hide (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Andresen, 2012).

The two sections belong together because each rule is the other face of a benefit. Moving the script to the spender makes it necessary to count the work it hides, and making the output opaque makes it possible to lock coins to a script that cannot be satisfied. A reader who knows both can say not only why P2SH was added but also what it costs.

The first section gives the benefits with the sizes recomputed for Mohammed's script; the second sets out the rules, runs each of them with the library and reports the policy limit of Bitcoin Core on the signature checks of a redeem script. The sections use BIP16 for the rules of 2012 and the source of Bitcoin Core at the pinned commit for the rules of today.

The rules were added to a live system with a soft fork, which means that an old node still accepts what the new rules reject. The BIP spends several paragraphs on the one-confirmation attack that this opens, and on the way miners were asked to signal support, which is why a part of this history appears in the stories of this chapter.

nodes.label: Benefits of P2SH
nodes.body: The benefits of P2SH are four, in the words of the book. The similarity to the original legacy addresses means that the sender and the sender's wallet need no complex engineering; the burden of storing the long script moves from the output, which is on the chain and in the set of unspent outputs, to the input, which is only on the chain; it moves from the present to a future time; and the transaction fee of a long script moves from the sender to the recipient (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The benefits of P2SH are four, in the words of the book. The similarity to the original legacy addresses means that the sender and the sender's wallet need no complex engineering; the burden of storing the long script moves from the output, which is on the chain and in the set of unspent outputs, to the input, which is only on the chain; it moves from the present to a future time; and the transaction fee of a long script moves from the sender to the recipient (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The first benefit made the second possible. Because the payer saw only an address, exchanges, shops and wallets that already knew how to pay an address could pay a multisignature without being changed, and BIP16 names that as its reason: it would minimize the changes needed to all of the supporting infrastructure and allow merchants and exchanges to support multisignature transactions sooner (Andresen, 2012). The storage benefit is a benefit to every node, since the long script does not sit in the set of unspent outputs.

The example counts the bytes for Mohammed's script with compressed keys: the 2-of-5 script is 173 bytes, the P2SH output script is 23 bytes, and the output of the payer is therefore 150 bytes shorter. The library recomputes the script size and also the size of the real spend, in which the spender adds the redeem script and two signatures; the spending input is the larger one, which is the shifting of the burden that the book describes.

The shifted cost is paid in the future. When the owners spend, their input script contains the empty dummy, the signatures and the full redeem script, so the transaction they pay a fee for is bigger than a spend of a single key. The fee is proportional to size, so the owner pays about the cost of the script that the payer did not. A group that wants to be paid in this way is choosing to carry the cost of its own security.

The fee shift is a shift, not a saving: in total the chain carries the same bytes. The book's remark that the payment is about five times larger without P2SH is a rough comparison with a simple payment which this page does not re-derive; the sizes of the script and the output are what it computes. And the opacity of the hash has a price, covered in the next section.

nodes.example: the long script moves from the payer to the spender
nodes.definition: P2SH makes a complex payment as easy as an ordinary one for the payer and shifts the storage and the fee of the long script to the later spender.

nodes.label: P2SH validation rules
nodes.body: The validation rules of pay to script hash come from BIP16 and from the code of Bitcoin Core. BIP16 lists them: validation fails if there are any operations other than push data operations in the input script; normal validation is done, and fails at once if the hash of the script does not match the output; and then the script is popped off the stack and validated again with the rest of the stack. The book adds that a P2SH cannot be put inside a P2SH redeem script because the specification is not recursive, and that OP_RETURN in a redeem script would make the transaction invalid (Andresen, 2012) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The validation rules of pay to script hash come from BIP16 and from the code of Bitcoin Core. BIP16 lists them: validation fails if there are any operations other than push data operations in the input script; normal validation is done, and fails at once if the hash of the script does not match the output; and then the script is popped off the stack and validated again with the rest of the stack. The book adds that a P2SH cannot be put inside a P2SH redeem script because the specification is not recursive, and that OP_RETURN in a redeem script would make the transaction invalid (Andresen, 2012) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The rules matter because they make an opaque output safe to validate. The push-only rule prevents an input script from changing what the redeem script means, and the single evaluation keeps the cost of a spend bounded. The counting rule exists because Bitcoin limits the signature checks per block to protect miners; BIP16 explains that without a limit a rogue miner might broadcast a block that requires hundreds of thousands of signature operations to validate and gain a head start on the next block (Andresen, 2012).

In Bitcoin Core the rules are in VerifyScript: a failure of the push-only rule is the error SIG_PUSHONLY, and a hash mismatch simply makes the first stage false. The counting rule has two forms. BIP16 counts a CHECKMULTISIG that follows a small number as that many operations and any other as 20, and the example applies it to the BIP's two examples to get 3 and 22. Bitcoin Core's relay policy also refuses an input if its redeem script contains more than 15 such operations, the constant MAX_P2SH_SIGOPS (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The library runs each rule. A redeem script that is OP_1 succeeds; the redeem script OP_0 fails with EVAL_FALSE; an input script that has an extra no-operation before the push fails with SIG_PUSHONLY; a redeem script whose hash does not match fails with EVAL_FALSE; and a redeem script that is itself a P2SH output script is not run as a P2SH again, it only has its hash compared, so that an inner script that would be false is never executed. With the P2SH flag switched off, as in the rules before 2012, even the always-false redeem script is accepted.

Not recursive is a surprise in one direction: the nested output is not evaluated, so a script hash inside a script hash does not protect the funds in the way a reader might expect. And invalid is a surprise in the other: the network accepts the creation of an output whose redeem script can never succeed, so a mistake is only discovered at the time of spending, when nothing can be changed. The book makes this a warning, and so does this page.

nodes.example: push-only input, no recursion, counted signature operations
nodes.definition: The validation rules of P2SH say that the input script may only push data, that the redeem script is run exactly once, with no further P2SH inside, and that the signature checks it hides are counted.

nodes.label: Data output and timelocks
nodes.body: This branch collects two kinds of condition that have nothing to do with keys. The first is an output that carries data and cannot be spent, the OP_RETURN output; the second is a set of conditions about time, which restrict when a transaction may be included in a block or when an output may be spent. The book treats them one after the other: the data recording output, the limits of a transaction lock time, the absolute timelock opcode OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, and the relative timelocks, the sequence field and OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch collects two kinds of condition that have nothing to do with keys. The first is an output that carries data and cannot be spent, the OP_RETURN output; the second is a set of conditions about time, which restrict when a transaction may be included in a block or when an output may be spent. The book treats them one after the other: the data recording output, the limits of a transaction lock time, the absolute timelock opcode OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, and the relative timelocks, the sequence field and OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Time is the one input to a script that every node can agree on, and the branch explains how it is brought in. A script is stateless, so it can not look at a clock; the transaction carries the numbers, a lock time and a sequence, and the opcodes compare them with the numbers in the script. Timelocks are the basis of savings plans, of inheritance and escrow arrangements with a deadline, and of payment channels, and the data output is the standard way to record a fingerprint of a document in the chain without creating an output that every node must remember (Todd, 2014) (BtcDrak et al., 2015).

In the 599 transactions saved from block 775,072 the data output and the lock time are both present: 8 outputs carry data, and 131 transactions set a lock time, of which 108 use the height of the preceding block; but none of the 91 witness scripts that were revealed uses a timelock opcode (mempool.space, 2026). The same block shows how far reality is from the examples of the book: wallets use the lock time field of the transaction as a protective measure, and timelocks as a feature of a script are rare.

The branch has three groups. The data output group shows what a provably unspendable output is and how Bitcoin Core's relay policy limits it. The absolute timelock group explains why a lock time alone does not bind the signer and how the opcode adds the missing guarantee. The relative timelock group explains the encoding of the sequence field and the opcode that reads it. The examples run on real signatures and on real transactions, and the activation dates come from the blocks at the heights in Bitcoin Core's chain parameters.

nodes.label: Recording data without bloat
nodes.body: This group is about outputs that exist only to carry data. The book describes the controversy: using the blockchain for data that is not payment, such as a commitment to a file as proof that it existed on a date, is considered abusive by some and a demonstration of the technology by others (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group is about outputs that exist only to carry data. The book describes the controversy: using the blockchain for data that is not payment, such as a commitment to a file as proof that it existed on a date, is considered abusive by some and a demonstration of the technology by others (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The two sections show a compromise between those views and its present setting. The OP_RETURN output costs the network disk space in the chain but not the more expensive memory and database space of the set of unspent outputs, and the relay policy of Bitcoin Core decides how many bytes of such data a transaction may carry. The group is a case of the difference between what the consensus rules allow and what nodes agree to relay.

The first section describes the output and what happens if an input tries to spend it, with the proof-of-existence prefix of the book and the real outputs of block 775,072. The second section reads the policy of Bitcoin Core at the pinned commit: a default that accepts data carriers, a size in vbytes derived from the standard weight, and the budget that is shared by all data outputs of a transaction.

The default of the policy is not a rule of the protocol. A miner may include any transaction that follows the consensus rules, including one that carries more data than the relay policy of its neighbours accept, and a user can change the default with a start-up option. The group therefore keeps the two apart each time a number appears.

nodes.label: OP_RETURN output
nodes.body: An OP_RETURN output is an output script of the form OP_RETURN followed by data. The book explains it as a compromise: it allows an output script that starts with OP_RETURN to add data that is not a payment to a transaction output, and unlike the use of fake outputs, which hide data in the 20 bytes of an address and can never be spent but stay in the database for ever, the output is explicitly provably unspendable and need not be stored in the set of unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An OP_RETURN output is an output script of the form OP_RETURN followed by data. The book explains it as a compromise: it allows an output script that starts with OP_RETURN to add data that is not a payment to a transaction output, and unlike the use of fake outputs, which hide data in the 20 bytes of an address and can never be spent but stay in the database for ever, the output is explicitly provably unspendable and need not be stored in the set of unspent outputs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The output matters because it separates the cost of data from the cost of payments. A fake output built from an address that corresponds to no private key bloats the database of every full node, which must remember it in case it is spent. An OP_RETURN output is recorded in the blockchain, so it uses disk space, but it is not stored in the set of unspent outputs and does not make the database operations more expensive. Bitcoin Core's function IsUnspendable says that a script is unspendable if it starts with OP_RETURN or is longer than the script size limit, so that the output can be pruned at once when it enters the set (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The data is often a hash such as the 32 bytes of SHA-256, sometimes with a prefix that identifies the application. The book gives the example of a notarization service that uses the 8-byte prefix DOCPROOF, written 44 4f 43 50 52 4f 4f 46 in hexadecimal; the example builds such an output script for the hash of a document and finds it 42 bytes long. Block 775,072 holds 8 data outputs among the 1,668 outputs of its first 599 transactions: 5 of 83 bytes whose first bytes push 80 bytes of data, and three shorter ones of 3, 55 and 54 bytes. Five of them carry a value of 5,500 or 6,213 satoshis (mempool.space, 2026).

The engine stops at once when it reaches the opcode. In Bitcoin Core's interpreter the case for OP_RETURN returns the error SCRIPT_ERR_OP_RETURN, so a script that executes it fails; the book puts it in words: if an OP_RETURN output is referenced as an input, the validation engine halts and marks the transaction invalid, and there is no input script that could spend it. The page's stack machine shows the same: a script that reaches RETURN fails whatever else is on the stack (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book says that OP_RETURN outputs usually have a zero amount, because any bitcoins assigned to such an output are lost for ever. The saved block shows that this is a habit and not a rule: five of its eight data outputs hold a few thousand satoshis, which are burned. The opcode also had a history as a bug: in the first versions of the software the opcode ended the evaluation of a script with success, a story the page tells in the branch on the language of Script.

nodes.example: OP_RETURN <data>
nodes.definition: An OP_RETURN output is an output whose script begins with OP_RETURN followed by data; it can never be spent, so nodes need not keep it in the set of unspent outputs.

nodes.label: Data carrier policy
nodes.body: The data carrier policy is the part of Bitcoin Core's relay rules that concerns outputs with data. The source declares a default that accepts data carriers, DEFAULT_ACCEPT_DATACARRIER, and a default size setting in vbytes, MAX_OP_RETURN_RELAY, which is the standard transaction weight of 400,000 divided by the witness scale factor of 4, that is 100,000. In the function that decides whether a transaction is standard, every output that is a data carrier takes its whole script size from a budget, and a transaction that exceeds the budget is refused with the reason datacarrier (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: The data carrier policy is the part of Bitcoin Core's relay rules that concerns outputs with data. The source declares a default that accepts data carriers, DEFAULT_ACCEPT_DATACARRIER, and a default size setting in vbytes, MAX_OP_RETURN_RELAY, which is the standard transaction weight of 400,000 divided by the witness scale factor of 4, that is 100,000. In the function that decides whether a transaction is standard, every output that is a data carrier takes its whole script size from a budget, and a transaction that exceeds the budget is refused with the reason datacarrier (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The policy is the answer to the controversy that the book describes. Those who want to discourage the use of the chain for data can limit what their node relays, and those who want to encourage it can raise the limit; the setting is a policy, which each node operator controls, and not a consensus rule. The book does not quote a number; this page reads the value in the source at the commit pinned for the course, and a later release may set another.

The budget is shared. Because the loop subtracts the size of each data output from one variable, two outputs of 60,000 and 50,000 bytes cannot both be relayed even though each is below the limit; the example runs this rule on the two sizes and the second one is refused. The eight data outputs of block 775,072 hold 527 bytes of script between them, which is far below the budget (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (mempool.space, 2026).

A relay node checks the transaction in the function IsStandardTx. For each output it first asks whether the script is standard at all; for a data carrier it takes the script size from the remaining budget and rejects the transaction if the size is larger than what is left; for a bare multisignature output it rejects the transaction unless the node permits bare multisignature. The same loop is why a transaction with several data outputs is judged by their total (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The word vbytes means virtual bytes, a measure of the weight of a transaction divided by four, which is the unit in which fees are priced; for a script outside the witness the vbytes are equal to the bytes. A policy limit is also not a promise that a transaction below it is relayed, since other rules, such as the fee rate, apply too. Because miners are not bound by the policy, a transaction that no node relays can still be mined when someone sends it to a miner directly.

nodes.definition: The data carrier policy is the relay rule that decides how many bytes of OP_RETURN data a transaction may carry; in Bitcoin Core it accepts data carriers by default and shares one budget of 100,000 vbytes among all the data outputs of a transaction.

nodes.label: Absolute timelocks
nodes.body: This group is about conditions that name a point in time or a block height. A transaction has a lock time, which restricts the blocks it can be included in, and a script can use the opcode OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY to restrict an output so that it is spent only by a transaction whose lock time has passed a given value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group is about conditions that name a point in time or a block height. A transaction has a lock time, which restricts the blocks it can be included in, and a script can use the opcode OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY to restrict an output so that it is spent only by a transaction whose lock time has passed a given value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The two mechanisms are different in who they bind. The lock time of a transaction binds nobody: whoever signed it can also sign a different transaction that spends the same inputs without a lock time. The opcode puts the restriction on the output itself, so that no transaction, signed by anyone, can spend the output before the time. The book builds this contrast in two sections, and so does the group.

The first section states the limitation of the lock time with the example of Alice and Bob and reads the rule of Bitcoin Core that decides whether a transaction with a given lock time can be in a block. The second section explains the opcode, runs it on real signatures, and notes how the activation dates of the soft forks are known from the blocks. The example numbers of the book are recomputed along the way.

Absolute means counted from a fixed point, the beginning of the chain or of the year 1970, not from the moment an output was created. A value below 500,000,000 is a block height and a value at or above it is a time in seconds since 1 January 1970, and the two kinds cannot be compared with each other.

nodes.label: Lock time limits
nodes.body: The lock time is the last field of a transaction, and the book explains its rules: a lock time of 0 means the transaction can be included in any block; a value below 500,000,000 restricts it to a block height, and a value of 500,000,000 or more is a time in seconds since the beginning of 1970 that the median time past of the block must exceed; this was added by Bitcoin's earliest known soft fork, starting at block height 31,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The limitation that the chapter explains is the one of a promise: the only guarantee a lock time gives is that the receiver cannot redeem the signed transaction before the time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The lock time is the last field of a transaction, and the book explains its rules: a lock time of 0 means the transaction can be included in any block; a value below 500,000,000 restricts it to a block height, and a value of 500,000,000 or more is a time in seconds since the beginning of 1970 that the median time past of the block must exceed; this was added by Bitcoin's earliest known soft fork, starting at block height 31,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The limitation that the chapter explains is the one of a promise: the only guarantee a lock time gives is that the receiver cannot redeem the signed transaction before the time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The limitation is why the opcode exists. In the book's example Alice signs a transaction paying Bob with a lock time three months ahead and gives it to Bob to hold. Bob cannot send it for three months and may send it afterwards; but Alice can create a conflicting transaction that spends the same inputs without a lock time and spend the output earlier, and Bob has no guarantee that she will not. The only way to guarantee that Bob receives the funds, but cannot spend them for three months, is to put the restriction on the output as part of the script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In practice wallets use the lock time for a different purpose. The saved block of 775,072 contains 131 transactions with a nonzero lock time among its first 599, and all 131 are heights below 500,000,000; 108 of them are 775,071, the height of the block before. The book's chapter on fees explains the reason: several wallets create transactions with a lock time that limits them to the next block or any later block, which discourages miners from rewriting history to take higher-fee transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (mempool.space, 2026).

The rule is in Bitcoin Core's function IsFinalTx. A transaction is final if its lock time is 0 or if the lock time is less than the height of the block (for a height) or the median time past of the block's predecessor (for a time); and even if not, it is final if every input has the sequence number 0xffffffff, which switches the lock time off. The example applies the first two conditions: a transaction with lock time 775,071 is final in block 775,072 and not final in block 775,071 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book states the rule as an equal-or-higher comparison, for example that a lock time of 123,456 can be included in block 123,456 or any later block; the source says less than, so that the block 123,456 is excluded and the first block that can include it is 123,457. A comment in the same file calls the lock time the last invalid height or time. The difference is one block, and the saved block agrees with the source: its transactions with lock time 775,071 sit in block 775,072. The sequence number 0xffffffff also matters: it disables the lock time, which is why the opcode in the next section checks it.

nodes.example: lock time stops a transaction, not a spender
nodes.definition: The lock time of a transaction restricts only when that transaction can be included in a block; it does not stop the signer from spending the same inputs in another transaction without a lock time.

nodes.label: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY
nodes.body: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, written CLTV in short, is an opcode that makes an output spendable only after a given block height or time. The book says it was introduced in December 2015 as a soft fork on the specification BIP65, that it is a per-output timelock where the lock time is per transaction, and that the output is restricted so it can be spent only in a transaction whose lock time is greater than or equal to the value in the script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Todd, 2014).

paras.text: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, written CLTV in short, is an opcode that makes an output spendable only after a given block height or time. The book says it was introduced in December 2015 as a soft fork on the specification BIP65, that it is a per-output timelock where the lock time is per transaction, and that the output is restricted so it can be spent only in a transaction whose lock time is greater than or equal to the value in the script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Todd, 2014).

The opcode closes the gap that the previous section described. With it, Alice sends her transaction at once, assigning the funds to Bob's key; she can no longer spend the money, and Bob cannot spend it before the three months have passed. BIP65 gives further uses: an escrow in which a lawyer can sign with one of two parties only after three months, refunds for payment channels that do not depend on the cooperation of the other party, and two-factor wallets in which the user can spend alone after an expiry time (Todd, 2014).

Bitcoin Core enforces the opcode from block 388,381, which was mined on 14 December 2015 and which has the hash that a comment in the chain parameters records; it is the first block at which the rule applied (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (mempool.space, 2026). The example script is the book's form, the signature check followed by the time and the opcode, wrapped in a script hash. The library signs it with a real key and runs it: a transaction with lock time 500,000 and a sequence that is not final succeeds, one with lock time 499,999 fails, and one whose sequence is final fails with UNSATISFIED_LOCKTIME.

The engine takes the number from the top of the stack, which may have up to five bytes, because four would end the usable range in the year 2038, and fails with a negative-lock-time error if the number is below zero. It then compares: the kinds must match, both a height or both a time; the number in the script must not exceed the lock time of the transaction; and the input's sequence must not be 0xffffffff. BIP65 lists exactly these conditions, plus the empty stack. If they hold, the opcode does nothing and the number stays on the stack, which is why scripts often have OP_DROP after it, as the book explains (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Todd, 2014) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The opcode redefined the existing no-operation opcode NOP2, and that is the source of its odd behaviour: old software treated the opcode as doing nothing, so the new behaviour had to be a restriction that old nodes do not enforce, a soft fork. The library shows what an old node would do: with the flag switched off it accepts a spend with lock time 0. The book gives the amount for three months as 12,960 blocks or 7,760,000 seconds; 12,960 blocks of ten minutes are exactly 90 days, but 90 days are 7,776,000 seconds, so the second figure is about 16,000 seconds short. And two calls of the opcode, one with a height and one with a time, can never both succeed in one script.

nodes.example: <pk> OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY <n> OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY
nodes.definition: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY fails a script unless the lock time of the spending transaction is of the same kind as, and at least as large as, the number on top of the stack, and the input is not final.

(lambda g: (exec("def cltv(n, lock, seq):                # the failure conditions of BIP65 that do not depend on the stack
    if n < 0: return 'fail'
    if (n < 500000000) != (lock < 500000000): return 'fail'
    if n > lock: return 'fail'
    if seq == 0xffffffff: return 'fail'
    return 'ok'
result = (cltv(500000, 500000, 0), cltv(500000, 499999, 0), cltv(500000, 500000, 0xffffffff), cltv(500000, 1700000000, 0))", g), g['result'])[1])({})

nodes.label: Relative timelocks
nodes.body: This group is about conditions that count time from the moment an output was confirmed. The book says that lock time and OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY are absolute timelocks, and the next two features are relative timelocks, which specify as a condition of spending an elapsed time since the confirmation of the output in the blockchain. The transaction-level form uses the sequence field of each input, and the script-level form is the opcode OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group is about conditions that count time from the moment an output was confirmed. The book says that lock time and OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY are absolute timelocks, and the next two features are relative timelocks, which specify as a condition of spending an elapsed time since the confirmation of the output in the blockchain. The transaction-level form uses the sequence field of each input, and the script-level form is the opcode OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A relative timelock allows a time constraint on one transaction that depends on the age of a previous transaction: the clock does not start until the output is recorded in the blockchain. This is what makes it possible to sign and keep a chain of transactions off the chain, since a child cannot be used until the parent has been mined and has aged, and it is the basis of the bidirectional payment channels and the Lightning Network that the book describes in a later chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The first section decodes the sequence field according to BIP68, with its flag bits and its unit of 512 seconds; the second explains the opcode of BIP112 that compares a number in the script with the sequence of the spending input, and runs it with real signatures. The activation of both is read from the block at the height in the chain parameters.

The sequence field has an older meaning that is still in use: the value 0xffffffff means a final input, and the lock time of a transaction is ignored if all inputs are final; the values just below it are used by wallets for other purposes. The new meaning applies only to transactions of version 2 or higher, and only if bit 31 of the field is clear.

nodes.label: Relative timelock (sequence)
nodes.body: A relative timelock is a restriction on an input that counts time from the confirmation of the output it spends. BIP68 repurposes the sequence number of each input for it. If bit 31 of the sequence is set, no consensus meaning is applied. If it is clear, the sequence is an encoded relative lock time: bit 22 decides whether the lock is in blocks, when the bit is clear, or in units of 512 seconds, when it is set, and only the low 16 bits, selected with the mask 0x0000ffff, carry the number (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

paras.text: A relative timelock is a restriction on an input that counts time from the confirmation of the output it spends. BIP68 repurposes the sequence number of each input for it. If bit 31 of the sequence is set, no consensus meaning is applied. If it is clear, the sequence is an encoded relative lock time: bit 22 decides whether the lock is in blocks, when the bit is clear, or in units of 512 seconds, when it is set, and only the low 16 bits, selected with the mask 0x0000ffff, carry the number (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The design gives a year of range and the same resolution in both units. BIP68 explains the 512 seconds: blocks come about every 600 seconds, so the same number of bits can encode the same amount of time whether it is counted in blocks or in time; converting a sequence to seconds means multiplying by 512, which is 2 to the power 9. With 16 bits the largest block lock is 65,535 blocks, about 455 days, and the largest time lock is 65,535 times 512 seconds, about 388 days. The rules apply only to transactions of version 2 or higher, and not to the coinbase (Friedenbach et al., 2015).

The encoding is in Bitcoin Core's header: the constants SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_DISABLE_FLAG as bit 31, SEQUENCE_LOCKTIME_TYPE_FLAG as bit 22, the mask 0x0000ffff and the granularity of 9. The page's example decodes four sequence numbers: 144 is a lock of 144 blocks, the value with bit 22 and the number 10 is 5,120 seconds, and the two values with bit 31 set, among them 0xfffffffd that wallets use for other purposes, have no relative lock. In block 775,072, among 594 inputs of version-2 transactions, only one has an enabled and nonzero relative lock (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (mempool.space, 2026).

The consensus code that applies the rule is the function CalculateSequenceLocks. For each input it finds the height of the block that confirmed the spent output, adds the number of blocks, or reads the median time past of the block before the confirming one and adds the number of 512-second units, and turns the result into the last invalid height and the last invalid time of the transaction, the same convention as for the lock time. The transaction can be in a block only if the block's height and the median time past of its predecessor are beyond both (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The block lock counts from the block that confirmed the output, and the time lock from the median time past of that block's predecessor, not from the time stamp of the block, so a time lock measured in 512-second units can be a few blocks off what a clock shows. And the commonly used values just below the maximum sequence have bit 31 set, so they are not relative locks at all; confusing the old and new meaning of the field is the usual mistake.

nodes.example: sequence 144 means: not before 144 blocks of age
nodes.definition: A relative timelock is encoded in the sequence field of an input: if bit 31 is clear, the low 16 bits are a number of blocks, or of 512-second units when bit 22 is set, that the spent output must have aged before the input is valid.

io.code:
(lambda g: (exec("def decode(seq):
    if seq & (1 << 31): return 'no relative lock'
    n = seq & 0xffff
    return (n * 512, 'seconds') if seq & (1 << 22) else (n, 'blocks')
result = [decode(s) for s in (144, (1 << 22) | 10, 1 << 31, 0xfffffffd)]", g), g['result'])[1])({})

nodes.label: OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY
nodes.body: OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, written CSV, is the script opcode for relative timelocks. The book says that, as with lock time and OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, there is an opcode for relative timelocks that reads the sequence value: when it is evaluated in the script of an output, the output can be spent only in a transaction whose input sequence is greater than or equal to the parameter, which restricts spending until a number of blocks or seconds have passed relative to the time the output was mined (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, written CSV, is the script opcode for relative timelocks. The book says that, as with lock time and OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, there is an opcode for relative timelocks that reads the sequence value: when it is evaluated in the script of an output, the output can be spent only in a transaction whose input sequence is greater than or equal to the parameter, which restricts spending until a number of blocks or seconds have passed relative to the time the output was mined (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The opcode lets a script decide by the age of the output. BIP112 gives an escrow with a timeout as its first example: three parties lock funds in a 2-of-3 script with an alternative branch, and after 30 days one of them can sign alone, but the clock does not start until the payment to the escrow address confirms. It also names hash time-locked contracts, bidirectional payment channels and the Lightning Network, where the delay gives a party a predictable time to respond when the other broadcasts an old state (BtcDrak et al., 2015).

BIP68 and BIP112 are enforced from block 419,328 of the chain, which was mined on 4 July 2016. The book says that they were activated in May 2016; the BIPs say the voting period started on 1 May 2016, and the rules applied from the later block that Bitcoin Core records (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (mempool.space, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The page's example runs the script with real signatures: with version 2 and a sequence of 144 the spend succeeds, a sequence of 143 fails, a version-1 transaction fails, and a sequence with bit 22 set fails because the kind differs. None of the 91 witness scripts revealed in block 775,072 contains the opcode, so the sampled block shows no use of it (mempool.space, 2026).

The engine reads the operand, which can have five bytes, fails if it is negative, and treats the opcode as a no-operation if the operand has the disable flag set, a hook for later soft forks. Otherwise it asks the checker to compare: the transaction version must be at least 2, the sequence of the input must not have bit 31 set, the kind bit must be the same in both, and the operand masked with the type bit and the 16-bit mask must not exceed the masked sequence. As for CLTV, the operand stays on the stack (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (BtcDrak et al., 2015).

The book points out a difference from CLTV: a script that executes several CSV opcodes must use only one kind, otherwise it can never be spent; but CSV allows any two valid inputs in one transaction, since each input has its own sequence, so the problem of interaction across inputs that exists for the absolute opcode does not occur. The opcode checks the sequence of the input and the sequence has to be set by the spender before signing, since the signature commits to it.

nodes.definition: OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY fails a script unless the transaction has version 2 or more and the sequence of the spending input carries a relative lock of the same kind as, and at least as large as, the number on top of the stack.
