nodes.label: Flow control and complex scripts
nodes.body: This branch is about scripts that have more than one way of being spent, and the tools for writing them. Flow control, also called conditional clauses, lets a script choose between code paths according to a true or false value that the spender supplies; the VERIFY opcodes attach preconditions; and nesting the conditionals produces scripts with many execution paths. The book ends the topic with a company's capital account that uses all these ideas together (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch is about scripts that have more than one way of being spent, and the tools for writing them. Flow control, also called conditional clauses, lets a script choose between code paths according to a true or false value that the spender supplies; the VERIFY opcodes attach preconditions; and nesting the conditionals produces scripts with many execution paths. The book ends the topic with a company's capital account that uses all these ideas together (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch is where Script becomes a language of contracts rather than of single keys. A script with several paths can express who may spend, when, and with whose help: partners who can act together at once, a lawyer who can help after a month, and the same lawyer who can act alone after three months. Every such rule is enforced by every node without a trusted party, which is what the book calls the power of the language.

The reader meets the pattern in the inheritance and recovery schemes of wallets, in escrow, in payment channels, and in the miniscript policies that tools produce. In the saved block of 775,072 none of the 91 witness scripts that were revealed contains a conditional, since all of them are multisignatures; the only conditional is in the one taproot spend that reveals a script, where the branch that follows OP_FALSE OP_IF is never executed and holds the bytes of an image (mempool.space, 2026). The sections run each script with real signatures, so that a reader sees which inputs reach which path.

The branch has two groups. The first, conditionals, covers the opcodes IF, NOTIF, ELSE and ENDIF, the guard clause made with a VERIFY opcode, and the selection of a path by the input script. The second, complex scripts, runs the capital-account script of the book on its three paths and then presents Miniscript, a structured language for the same kind of script that the tools of today use and that can be analysed by a program.

nodes.label: Conditionals and guards
nodes.body: This group covers the three ways a script decides what to do. A conditional clause chooses between two code paths; a VERIFY guard continues only if a condition holds; and a nest of conditionals offers many paths, one of which the spender selects in the input script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers the three ways a script decides what to do. A conditional clause chooses between two code paths; a VERIFY guard continues only if a condition holds; and a nest of conditionals offers many paths, one of which the spender selects in the input script (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because the condition is not part of the script. The output script contains the rules, and the input script contains the choice. This is how a single output can be spent in several different ways without anyone revealing, when the output is created, which way will be used.

The first section explains the IF construct and its reversed order, the second the guard clause and the reason it is preferred when there is a single path, and the third the maze of paths that nesting produces. The examples are run by the page's small stack machine and by the chapter's library on real signatures.

Reading the order is the hard part, because the condition comes before the IF, and the value at the top of the stack is the one the first IF takes. A beginner who reads a script as if it were a program in a common language often chooses the wrong path, which is why the book advises running small scripts on paper.

nodes.label: Conditional clauses
nodes.body: A conditional clause is the flow control of Script. The book says that Bitcoin's conditional opcodes allow a script that has two ways of being unlocked, depending on a true or false outcome of a logical condition: if the condition is true, one path is executed and otherwise the ELSE path. They are implemented with the opcodes OP_IF, OP_ELSE, OP_ENDIF and OP_NOTIF, together with boolean operators such as OP_BOOLAND, OP_BOOLOR and OP_NOT (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A conditional clause is the flow control of Script. The book says that Bitcoin's conditional opcodes allow a script that has two ways of being unlocked, depending on a true or false outcome of a logical condition: if the condition is true, one path is executed and otherwise the ELSE path. They are implemented with the opcodes OP_IF, OP_ELSE, OP_ENDIF and OP_NOTIF, together with boolean operators such as OP_BOOLAND, OP_BOOLOR and OP_NOT (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Conditionals turn a script into a decision with alternatives. The book adds that the clauses can be nested indefinitely, that scripts with hundreds of possible paths can be built, and that there is no limit to the nesting except the consensus limit on the size of a script in bytes. Without them a script could only be a single chain of checks, all of which would have to pass.

The reader meets conditionals in every script with alternatives; the example runs the book's construct on the page. The same three words of script are run with a true and a false condition on the stack: with 1 the first arm leaves 10, with 0 the second arm leaves 20, and the opposite opcode OP_NOTIF, which takes the first arm when the condition is false, leaves 20 for the value 1. Bitcoin Core's interpreter holds a list of flags, one for each open IF, which says whether the code now being read is executed (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book points out that the form looks backward, like 1 1 OP_ADD does: in a stack language the condition comes before the IF. The opcode takes the top item off the stack, treats any nonzero value as true, and starts an arm; OP_ELSE switches to the other arm; OP_ENDIF closes the clause. In the inactive arm the opcodes are read but not run, which is why a script with an unbalanced IF fails with its own error. Bitcoin Core's comment gives the pattern in the usual order, the expression, then if, the statements, else and endif (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The value that the IF takes can be any bytes, and the three kinds of script treat it differently. In the original rules every nonzero value is true. A policy rule for witness scripts, MINIMALIF, requires exactly an empty value or the single byte 1, and tapscript makes the same rule a consensus rule, with its own error. A wallet that wants its spends to be relayed as well as valid should therefore use OP_TRUE and OP_FALSE, as the book does, and not an arbitrary nonzero number.

nodes.example: <condition> OP_IF <A> OP_ELSE <B> OP_ENDIF
nodes.definition: A conditional clause is a group of opcodes between OP_IF or OP_NOTIF and OP_ENDIF, with an optional OP_ELSE, that runs one of two code paths according to the value on top of the stack when the OP_IF is reached.

nodes.label: VERIFY guard clause
nodes.body: A VERIFY guard is the second form of conditional in Script: any opcode that ends in VERIFY. The book explains that the suffix means that if the evaluated condition is not true, execution of the script terminates at once and the transaction is deemed invalid. Unlike an IF clause, which offers alternative paths, the suffix acts as a guard clause, continuing only if a precondition is met (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A VERIFY guard is the second form of conditional in Script: any opcode that ends in VERIFY. The book explains that the suffix means that if the evaluated condition is not true, execution of the script terminates at once and the transaction is deemed invalid. Unlike an IF clause, which offers alternative paths, the suffix acts as a guard clause, continuing only if a precondition is met (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The guard is the cheaper way to say that two things must both hold. The book's example requires Bob's signature and a preimage, a secret that produces a specific hash: the script hashes the first item, compares it with the expected hash and stops if they differ, and only then checks the signature; without the preimage, Bob cannot get to the part of the script that checks his signature. The same script can be written with OP_IF, but the VERIFY form uses two fewer opcodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets VERIFY in OP_EQUALVERIFY, which every pay to public key hash script uses, and in OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY, OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY and OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY. The page runs a guard with the hash function that the stack machine has: the script hashes the top item with SHA-256, compares it with a given digest and then leaves 1 on the stack. The secret abc passes, the secret abd stops with the failure of the guard, and the word counts of the two forms in the book's example are 5 and 7.

The engine implements the plain opcode OP_VERIFY as follows: it takes the top item, and if it is true removes it and goes on; if it is false it returns the error SCRIPT_ERR_VERIFY. The other opcodes with the suffix do the same after their own operation, as OP_EQUALVERIFY does after comparing two items (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's rule of thumb: if all you want is to attach a precondition, VERIFY is better; if you want more than one execution path, you need IF and ELSE (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two opcodes do not behave like the others with the suffix. OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY and OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY leave their operand on the stack, because the soft forks that added them redefined opcodes that did not drop items and the old behaviour had to be kept, so a script that uses them is followed by OP_DROP if the operand is in the way. The guard also does not choose: a script made only of guards has exactly one way of being spent.

nodes.example: OP_HASH160 <hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY <pk> OP_CHECKSIG
nodes.definition: An opcode with the suffix VERIFY ends the script with failure unless its result is true, and otherwise continues; it acts as a guard clause that attaches one precondition without offering a second path.

nodes.label: Scripts with several paths
nodes.body: A script with several paths is one in which the output offers more than one way to be redeemed. The book's first example has two signers, Alice and Bob, either of whom can redeem, written with an IF instead of a 1-of-2 multisignature: OP_IF with Alice's key, OP_ELSE with Bob's key, OP_ENDIF and OP_CHECKSIG. It then asks where the condition is, and answers that the condition is not part of the script; it is offered at spending time, so that Alice and Bob can choose which path they want (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A script with several paths is one in which the output offers more than one way to be redeemed. The book's first example has two signers, Alice and Bob, either of whom can redeem, written with an IF instead of a 1-of-2 multisignature: OP_IF with Alice's key, OP_ELSE with Bob's key, OP_ENDIF and OP_CHECKSIG. It then asks where the condition is, and answers that the condition is not part of the script; it is offered at spending time, so that Alice and Bob can choose which path they want (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The choice is made by the spender and not by the script, and that is a form of privacy and flexibility: the paths not taken are invisible until they are used, in a script hash output. The book generalizes: since OP_IF clauses can be nested, one can create a maze of execution paths, and the input script provides a map that selects which path is executed; with this construct, redeem scripts with tens or hundreds of paths can be built (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book's three-path script has subscripts A, B and C. To choose B the input script ends with OP_1 OP_0, true and false: the values are pushed so that the false is on top, the outer IF pops it and runs the first ELSE, and then the true moves to the top and is read by the inner IF, which selects B. The example runs the script for the three choices on the page and gets 10, 20 and 30 for A, B and C. The page's library does the same with Alice's and Bob's keys and real signatures: either path succeeds with its own signature, and a signature given to the wrong path fails.

The engine keeps a list of flags for the open clauses, and it pops one value for each IF that it reaches in an executed arm; the inner IF is only reached if the outer arm that contains it runs. That is why the choices appear in the reverse order of the clauses, the innermost first in the sense of being read last and pushed first. The order of the input script is the opposite of the order of reading, which is the reason the book's tip asks whether FALSE then TRUE is not backward, and answers that TRUE is pushed on top and therefore popped first (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A path that is never chosen is still part of the script. Its keys and its timelocks are all committed to by the hash of the script, and the script is revealed in full when any path is used, at least in a script hash output, so the existence of the other paths is made public by the spend. Taproot, in a later branch, was designed to avoid that. Also, a script with many paths takes space: every unused path is paid for in the fee of the transaction that uses the script.

nodes.example: <signature> OP_1 OP_0 selects path B
nodes.definition: A script with several paths nests conditional clauses so that each path is a different way to redeem the output, and the input script selects the path by pushing a true or false value for each clause.

nodes.label: Script with timelocks and signers
nodes.body: This group puts the previous branches together. The book's complex script example is a company capital account that has different rules depending on the time that has passed, with three partners who decide by majority and a lawyer who can help or replace them. Miniscript is the language that tools use today to write and analyse such scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2023).

paras.text: This group puts the previous branches together. The book's complex script example is a company capital account that has different rules depending on the time that has passed, with three partners who decide by majority and a lawyer who can help or replace them. Miniscript is the language that tools use today to write and analyse such scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2023).

The two sections show two stages of the same work. The first reads a script as a person would write it by hand, with the IF structure, the timelocks and the CHECKMULTISIG, and runs it with real signatures on all three paths. The second shows the rules by which a script like that can be built from small parts whose behaviour is known, so that the whole can be checked by a program and not only by a reader.

The first section executes the redeem script of the book's listing with the library; the days of the listing are written as blocks, 4,320 for 30 days and 12,960 for 90, as a block is a tenth of an hour. The second section reads the translation table of BIP379 and compiles two small examples by its rules, and then runs them.

A script that works on paper may not be spendable in practice. It may mix a timelock of heights with one of times, it may exceed a size limit, or it may need a signature order that the wallet does not produce. The group is meant to show both the power of the language and the reason why tools were built to check scripts.

nodes.label: Capital account script
nodes.body: The capital-account script is the book's combined example. Mohammed, a company owner in Dubai, wants a capital account with flexible rules: the participants are Mohammed, his two partners Saeed and Zaira, and the company lawyer; two of the three partners decide by majority; if there is a problem with their keys, the lawyer can recover the funds with one of the three partner signatures; and if all partners are unavailable or incapacitated for a while, the lawyer can manage the account directly. The redeem script nests two IF clauses and has three paths (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The capital-account script is the book's combined example. Mohammed, a company owner in Dubai, wants a capital account with flexible rules: the participants are Mohammed, his two partners Saeed and Zaira, and the company lawyer; two of the three partners decide by majority; if there is a problem with their keys, the lawyer can recover the funds with one of the three partner signatures; and if all partners are unavailable or incapacitated for a while, the lawyer can manage the account directly. The redeem script nests two IF clauses and has three paths (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The script shows how rules about people become rules about keys and time. The first path is an ordinary 2-of-3 multisignature that can be used at any time. The second can be used only after 30 days have passed since the output was confirmed, and requires the lawyer and one of the three partners, a 1-of-3 combined with a signature check. The third lets the lawyer spend alone but only after 90 days. The time conditions are relative, so the clock starts when the funds are confirmed, as the escrow of BIP112 does (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (BtcDrak et al., 2015).

The library builds the script with four demonstration keys, 30 days written as 4,320 blocks and 90 days as 12,960 blocks. The script is 192 bytes. It is spent on all three paths as a witness script hash and as a script hash. Path 1 with the signatures of the first and the third partner succeeds at once. Path 2 with the second partner and the lawyer succeeds with a sequence of 4,320 and fails with 4,319. Path 3 with the lawyer succeeds with a sequence of 12,960 and fails with 12,959. The signature of a partner on the third path does not help.

The inputs of the book are, for the first path, OP_0 then two partner signatures and OP_TRUE OP_TRUE; for the second, OP_0, a partner's signature, the lawyer's signature, OP_FALSE and OP_TRUE; and for the third the lawyer's signature and OP_FALSE. The leading OP_0 is the dummy element of the multisignature oddity. In the second path the lawyer's signature is checked first, by OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY with the lawyer's key, and the rest is a multisignature of one among three. The timelock comparisons are performed by OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY against the sequence of the spending input, and the transaction must have version 2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The book writes the delays as 30 days and 90 days; in the script they must be numbers, of blocks or of units of 512 seconds, and the two paths must use the same kind or the script becomes impossible to use for some inputs. Signatures must also be in the order of the keys: the library shows that the first and third partner succeed in that order and fail when the order is reversed. And the timelock is checked per input, so the script depends on the transaction version: with version 1 the third path never succeeds.

nodes.example: 2-of-3 partners, or lawyer plus one after 30 days, or lawyer after 90
nodes.definition: The capital-account script of the book has three execution paths: two of three partners at any time, the lawyer with one partner after 30 days, and the lawyer alone after 90 days, selected by two true or false values in the input script.

nodes.label: Miniscript
nodes.body: Miniscript is a language for writing a subset of Bitcoin Scripts in a structured way, enabling analysis, composition, generic signing and more, in the words of BIP379. The BIP says that Script is an unusual stack-based language with many edge cases, and that it is highly nontrivial to find the most economical script for a combination of spending conditions, to compose two scripts, to find out what spending conditions a script permits, or to know whether a limit such as the operation count might be hit. Miniscript gives a representation in which these operations are possible (Wuille et al., 2023).

paras.text: Miniscript is a language for writing a subset of Bitcoin Scripts in a structured way, enabling analysis, composition, generic signing and more, in the words of BIP379. The BIP says that Script is an unusual stack-based language with many edge cases, and that it is highly nontrivial to find the most economical script for a combination of spending conditions, to compose two scripts, to find out what spending conditions a script permits, or to know whether a limit such as the operation count might be hit. Miniscript gives a representation in which these operations are possible (Wuille et al., 2023).

The language answers the problem that the book's own example has. A hand-written script can contain a mistake, such as a height timelock mixed with a time timelock in one path, that makes the output unspendable. The book warns of this and advises thorough tests on a test network or a tool designed to prevent the issue, like a Miniscript compiler. BIP379 has a type system with a property for exactly this, named k, which means that no timelock of the same type is mixed height and time, and other properties for signatures and malleability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2023).

BIP379 has the status Draft, and Bitcoin Core's documentation records that it was partially implemented in release 24.0 and fully as of 26.0, which is the release that added tapscript. The fragments are used in output script descriptors, wsh() for witness script hash outputs and tr() for taproot. The page's example follows the translation table: pk(A) is the key followed by CHECKSIG, older(144) is 144 followed by CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY, the wrapper v: replaces the last opcode with its VERIFY form, and and_v and or_i give the concatenation and the IF form. The result is the script of the line above (Wuille et al., 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The chapter's library applies the same table to bytes and runs the result with real signatures: the first key can spend at once with the signature and a true value, and the second key can spend only after 144 blocks, with a false value, version 2 and a sequence of at least 144. The same code compiles a multi() fragment, the 2-of-3 multisignature, and the test that the compiled bytes equal those of the library's own multisignature builder passes. The check is of the table as printed in the BIP and not of Bitcoin Core's compiler, which was not available in this environment.

The BIP says that its specification applies to P2WSH and tapscript scripts, and that P2SH and bare scripts are excluded. It also lists the limits that a static analysis should check: in P2WSH, scripts larger than 3,600 bytes are invalid by standardness, an operation count above 201 is invalid by consensus, and a stack above 1,000 elements is invalid in both. Miniscript is not a different way of spending; the output on the chain is an ordinary script, and what changes is the confidence with which it was made.

nodes.example: or_i(pk(A),and_v(v:pk(B),older(144)))
nodes.definition: Miniscript is a structured way of writing a subset of Bitcoin Script, in which small fragments with known behaviour are composed by rules, so that a program can analyse the result, find the spending conditions and construct witnesses.

nodes.label: Segregated witness scripts
nodes.body: This branch is about the outputs that came with segregated witness, the upgrade of 2017 that moved the proofs of authorization out of the part of a transaction that identifies it. A segregated witness output script is two pushes, a version number and a short program, and it is spent with a witness structure instead of an input script. The branch covers the two programs of version 0, pay to witness public key hash and pay to witness script hash, their addresses, the way old and new software live together, the nested forms, and the new signature hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch is about the outputs that came with segregated witness, the upgrade of 2017 that moved the proofs of authorization out of the part of a transaction that identifies it. A segregated witness output script is two pushes, a version number and a short program, and it is spent with a witness structure instead of an input script. The branch covers the two programs of version 0, pay to witness public key hash and pay to witness script hash, their addresses, the way old and new software live together, the nested forms, and the new signature hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The upgrade matters because most of the bitcoin that moves today is spent this way. In the 1,022 inputs of block 775,072's first 599 transactions, 626 spend a native witness key hash output and 57 a native witness script hash output, and another 129 spend the same programs nested in a script hash, against 194 legacy key hash inputs: 812 of the 1,022 inputs, about 79 percent, are segwit forms (mempool.space, 2026). They are cheaper than their legacy equivalents, and they removed the signature from the data that a third party could change to alter a transaction identifier (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

A reader meets the forms as addresses that begin with bc1q, or with 3 for the nested forms, and as the line in a decoded transaction where the witness appears after the outputs. The branch runs a real spend of every form with the library, so that each statement about what the engine does with a program is a result and not a description. All of it is backed by the specification BIP141 and the code of Bitcoin Core (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The first, witness programs, defines the program and its two version-0 forms and the address format that carries them. The second, the upgrade, explains why old software accepts the new outputs, how the nested forms let a payer who knows nothing of segwit pay a segwit wallet, and what the new signature hash changes. The activation height of 481,824 and its date come from the saved block.

nodes.label: Witness programs and addresses
nodes.body: This group defines the new kind of output and shows its three faces: the output script, the witness that spends it, and the address that carries it. A witness program is a version and a hash; the hash is of a public key or of a script; and the address is a checksummed text that carries the same two things (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Wuille et al., 2017).

paras.text: This group defines the new kind of output and shows its three faces: the output script, the witness that spends it, and the address that carries it. A witness program is a version and a hash; the hash is of a public key or of a script; and the address is a checksummed text that carries the same two things (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Wuille et al., 2017).

The faces correspond to three kinds of reader. A node reads the output script, a wallet builds the witness, and a person reads and types the address. The design makes each face as simple as the job allows: the output script is shorter than its legacy equivalent, the witness holds exactly the data that the program needs, and the address is easier to read aloud and to scan than the legacy address.

The first section defines the program and the rule that decides what it means from its version and length; the second and third give the key hash and script hash forms with real spends and the failures that follow from breaking each rule; the fourth builds the address, with the algorithm in a few lines that the page runs.

A witness program is never created by converting a key or an address that was meant for something else. The book is explicit that the receiver must create it, since the sender cannot know whether the receiver's wallet can spend such an output. The same care applies to the choice of key: only a compressed public key is safe.

nodes.label: Witness program
nodes.body: A witness program is what BIP141 calls an output script that consists of a one-byte push opcode, one of OP_0 and OP_1 to OP_16, followed by a direct data push between 2 and 40 bytes. The value of the first push is the version byte, and the following byte vector is the witness program. The book explains the same in its own words: to an old client the two pushes look like an output that anyone can spend, while to a segwit-aware client the first number is the witness version and the second part is the witness program (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A witness program is what BIP141 calls an output script that consists of a one-byte push opcode, one of OP_0 and OP_1 to OP_16, followed by a direct data push between 2 and 40 bytes. The value of the first push is the version byte, and the following byte vector is the witness program. The book explains the same in its own words: to an old client the two pushes look like an output that anyone can spend, while to a segwit-aware client the first number is the witness version and the second part is the witness program (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The definition is what lets one structure carry several kinds of authorization. With the version byte 0, the length of the program tells the two forms apart: 20 bytes is the hash of a key, 32 bytes the hash of a script, and any other length fails. Versions 1 to 16 are reserved for future extensions with no restriction: taproot is version 1. The book gives the length as the one difference that lets a full node tell the two version-0 programs apart (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

Bitcoin Core's function IsWitnessProgram applies the rule: the script must be 4 to 42 bytes long, begin with OP_0 or OP_1 to OP_16, and have a second byte equal to the length of what follows. The page's example classifies five scripts by the rule: a 20-byte program is P2WPKH, a 32-byte one P2WSH, a 19-byte version-0 program fails, a 32-byte version-1 program is taproot, and a version-16 program is a future version. The library does the same on real spends (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The engine runs the output script first, which pushes the version and the program, then recognises the pattern and does not run anything else for it; it hands the witness to VerifyWitnessProgram. There the version and the size select the case, in the code of Bitcoin Core: a 32-byte program is a script hash, a 20-byte program a key hash, and any other size of a version-0 program is the error WITNESS_PROGRAM_WRONG_LENGTH. The input script must be exactly empty, otherwise validation fails; for a witness program inside a script hash it must be exactly a push of the redeem script (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

A detail of the first execution makes some programs fail early. Because the engine runs the output script on its own first, the program is on top of the stack, and a program whose bytes are all zero counts as false, so the script fails before the witness is looked at; BIP141 notes that having a hash like this would be a preimage attack on the hash function and the risk is negligible. A program of 19 bytes with a nonzero byte fails with the length error, and a program of 41 bytes is not a witness program at all.

nodes.example: OP_0 <20 bytes> or OP_0 <32 bytes>
nodes.definition: A witness program is an output script made of a version byte (OP_0, or OP_1 to OP_16) followed by one push of 2 to 40 bytes; the version and the length of the program decide how the output is spent.

nodes.label: Pay to witness public key hash
nodes.body: A pay to witness public key hash output, P2WPKH, is the segregated witness equivalent of the pay to public key hash output. The book shows both for the same key hash ab68...: the legacy script has five items, and the witness one is 0 followed by the hash. It is much simpler: two values pushed onto the stack, the first the witness version and the second the witness program, which is simply the hash of the public key. Its spending transaction has an empty input script and a witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A pay to witness public key hash output, P2WPKH, is the segregated witness equivalent of the pay to public key hash output. The book shows both for the same key hash ab68...: the legacy script has five items, and the witness one is 0 followed by the hash. It is much simpler: two values pushed onto the stack, the first the witness version and the second the witness program, which is simply the hash of the public key. Its spending transaction has an empty input script and a witness structure (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The form does the same job for less: the output script is 22 bytes instead of 25, and the signature and the key sit in the witness, which gets a discount in the size on which the fee is calculated. BIP141 specifies it exactly: the witness must consist of exactly two items of at most 520 bytes each, a signature then a public key; the hash of the key must match the 20-byte program; and the signature is verified against the key with the signature check, which must leave a single true (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The form is the most common input of the saved block: 626 of the 1,022 inputs spend a P2WPKH output, three times more than the 194 legacy key hash inputs (mempool.space, 2026). The page's example builds the output script and the signed script code from the hash 751e76e8..., the key hash of BIP173's example key, and gets 22 bytes and 25 bytes. The library runs a real spend: it signs with the second demonstration key and verifies. Bitcoin Core builds the same script at run time, as DUP HASH160, the program, EQUALVERIFY and CHECKSIG (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The engine takes the two witness items as the initial stack, signature then key, and executes the implied legacy script on them, so a P2WPKH spend is a P2PKH spend with the data moved to the witness. If the witness does not have exactly two items, the error is WITNESS_PROGRAM_MISMATCH. The signature does not sign the legacy way: the code that is signed is the legacy key hash script, with its length byte, and the amount of the output is part of the hash, as the last section of the branch explains (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Lau et al., 2016).

The book's warnings are about the key. A P2WPKH program must be created by the receiver and never converted by the sender from a key, a P2PKH script or an address, and it must be built from the hash of a compressed public key; an uncompressed key is nonstandard and may be disabled by a soft fork, and funds sent to the hash of an uncompressed key may be lost. The library shows the first stage of this: a spend with an uncompressed key is valid by consensus, but is rejected when the policy flag WITNESS_PUBKEYTYPE is on, as in the standard flags (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: 0 <20-byte public key hash>
nodes.definition: A P2WPKH output holds a version 0 and the 20-byte hash of a compressed public key; it is spent by a witness of exactly two items, a signature and the public key, and an empty input script.

nodes.label: Pay to witness script hash
nodes.body: A pay to witness script hash output, P2WSH, is the segregated witness equivalent of pay to script hash. The book takes it from the multisignature of Mohammed's company: the output script is 0 followed by the 32-byte hash of the witness script, and the spend puts the signatures and the script in the witness, with an empty input script. The segregated witness script is a lot simpler than the legacy one and reduces the template overhead of the legacy form (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A pay to witness script hash output, P2WSH, is the segregated witness equivalent of pay to script hash. The book takes it from the multisignature of Mohammed's company: the output script is 0 followed by the 32-byte hash of the witness script, and the spend puts the signatures and the script in the witness, with an empty input script. The segregated witness script is a lot simpler than the legacy one and reduces the template overhead of the legacy form (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The hash is different, on purpose. The book explains that P2SH uses the 20-byte RIPEMD160(SHA256(script)) while P2WSH uses a 32-byte SHA256(script), deliberately, to give stronger security in certain use cases: 128 bits of security instead of 80. The change raises the cost of finding two scripts with the same hash, which matters when several parties build a script together. BIP141 adds that a witness script may be up to 10,000 bytes, since the 520-byte push limit does not apply to it, though each other witness item is at most 520 bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The page's example hashes BIP173's example script, a key followed by OP_CHECKSIG, once with SHA-256 and gets 1863143c...; with the version byte and the length it is the program of the address bc1qrp33g0q5... that BIP173 lists. In block 775,072, 57 of the inputs spend a P2WSH output directly and 34 more spend it nested; all 91 reveal a multisignature script (mempool.space, 2026). Bitcoin Core's standardness rules limit a witness script to 3,600 bytes, a stack of 100 items and 80 bytes per item (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The engine pops the last witness item, hashes it with a single SHA-256, compares it with the program, and if the hash differs it fails with WITNESS_PROGRAM_MISMATCH; an empty witness fails with WITNESS_PROGRAM_WITNESS_EMPTY. It then runs the script with the remaining items as the initial stack, in the witness version 0 rules, which differ from the legacy ones in two ways: the signature hash of BIP143 is used, and the signature is not removed from the script code. The result must be exactly one true on the stack (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The standard limits are not the consensus limits, and the difference can lock coins. A witness script of 10,000 bytes is valid by consensus, but Bitcoin Core relays only scripts up to 3,600 bytes; the library spends a 20-of-20 multisignature, which has 685 bytes, and a 15-of-15 in a script hash, both accepted. The book also warns that a P2WSH multisignature should be made by the receiver's wallet, as for the key hash form, and that the program is not the script, so the script has to be backed up.

nodes.label: Segwit address (bech32)
nodes.body: A native segregated witness address is a way to write a witness program that a person can read, type and scan. BIP173 defines the format, which it calls Bech32: a string of at most 90 characters made of a human-readable part, which for Bitcoin is bc on the main network, a separator that is always the character 1, and a data part of characters from a 32-character set that leaves out 1, b, i and o. The data part ends in a six-character checksum. The witness version is the first character of the data: q for 0 and p for 1 (Wuille et al., 2017).

paras.text: A native segregated witness address is a way to write a witness program that a person can read, type and scan. BIP173 defines the format, which it calls Bech32: a string of at most 90 characters made of a human-readable part, which for Bitcoin is bc on the main network, a separator that is always the character 1, and a data part of characters from a 32-character set that leaves out 1, b, i and o. The data part ends in a six-character checksum. The witness version is the first character of the data: q for 0 and p for 1 (Wuille et al., 2017).

The format fixes problems of the legacy addresses, which BIP173 lists: Base58 needs a lot of space in QR codes because it cannot use the alphanumeric mode, mixed case is inconvenient to write down and to read out, and the checksum from double SHA-256 is slow and has no error-detection guarantees. The new checksum is a BCH code, hence the name. BIP350 later found a weakness in the checksum for programs of later versions, and changed the constant for versions 1 and above, a variant called Bech32m, while version 0 keeps the original (Wuille et al., 2017) (Wuille, 2020).

The two BIPs give examples. For the key 0279BE66..., whose HASH160 is 751e76e8..., the main-network P2WPKH address is bc1qw508d6qejxtdg4y5r3zarvary0c5xw7kv8f3t4, and the page's example computes it in the browser from the hash. A version-1 program of 32 bytes, the x-coordinate 79be66... of the same key, gives bc1p0xlxvlhemja6c4dqv22uapctqupfhlxm9h8z3k2e72q4k9hcz7vqzk5jj0, a BIP350 vector, and the example computes that as well. The saved block's outputs are 754 P2WPKH, 69 P2WSH and 33 P2TR (Wuille, 2020) (mempool.space, 2026).

The algorithm has four steps. The witness version and the program bytes are regrouped from 8-bit bytes to 5-bit characters; the human-readable part is expanded into a list of values; a polynomial checksum over the expanded part and the data, followed by six zeros, is computed and combined with a constant, 1 for version 0 and 0x2bc830a3 for later versions; and the characters are looked up in the 32-character set. A decoder recomputes the checksum with the constant of the version and rejects the address on a mismatch (Wuille et al., 2017) (Wuille, 2020).

A legacy address and a bech32 address of the same key are different outputs, and an address must be entered in the form the wallet gives. The two constants matter: the BIP350 vector with the version-1 program written with the version-0 constant is invalid, and the library rejects it, as it does a changed last character. The address is also case-insensitive, but only if it is all lowercase or all uppercase; mixed case is invalid, which the specification gives as a reason to prefer an all-uppercase address in a QR code.

nodes.example: bc1q... carries a version-0 program, bc1p... a version-1 program
nodes.definition: A native segregated witness address writes the witness version and the program as a bech32 string with a human-readable part, a separator, 5-bit characters and a six-character checksum; version 0 uses bech32 and version 1 and later use bech32m.

nodes.label: Upgrading to segregated witness
nodes.body: This group explains how a system with millions of users changed its rules without stopping. Segregated witness was implemented as a backward-compatible upgrade in which old and new clients coexist; wallets upgraded independently; and outputs from the nested forms let a payer who knows nothing about segwit pay one who does. The new signature hash fixed two weaknesses of the old one at the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Lau et al., 2016).

paras.text: This group explains how a system with millions of users changed its rules without stopping. Segregated witness was implemented as a backward-compatible upgrade in which old and new clients coexist; wallets upgraded independently; and outputs from the nested forms let a payer who knows nothing about segwit pay one who does. The new signature hash fixed two weaknesses of the old one at the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (Lau et al., 2016).

The group matters because the way of introducing a change decides whether it is safe. A soft fork makes the rules stricter, so blocks valid under the new rules are valid under the old ones, and the old nodes follow the chain without understanding the new outputs. The price is that the old nodes see the new outputs as spendable by anyone, and the protection depends on the new nodes enforcing the rules.

The first section describes the soft fork and its two steps, with an old-node model; the second the nested forms, with their hashes and addresses recomputed from the book; the third the signature hash, with a model in the browser that is checked against the library.

The group describes the situation at a time. Native witness outputs are now the default of most wallets, and the nested forms are kept for payers whose software cannot yet send to a bech32 address; the saved block shows 129 nested inputs and 683 native witness inputs.

nodes.label: Backward-compatible upgrade
nodes.body: Segregated witness was implemented as a backward-compatible upgrade, where, in the book's phrase, old and new clients can coexist. Wallet developers independently upgraded wallet software to add segwit capabilities, while legacy P2PKH and P2SH continued to work for nonupgraded wallets. Two scenarios needed an answer: a spender's wallet that is not segwit-aware must be able to pay a recipient who can process segwit, and a segwit-aware wallet must be able to tell the recipients that are segwit-aware from the others, by their addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Segregated witness was implemented as a backward-compatible upgrade, where, in the book's phrase, old and new clients can coexist. Wallet developers independently upgraded wallet software to add segwit capabilities, while legacy P2PKH and P2SH continued to work for nonupgraded wallets. Two scenarios needed an answer: a spender's wallet that is not segwit-aware must be able to pay a recipient who can process segwit, and a segwit-aware wallet must be able to tell the recipients that are segwit-aware from the others, by their addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism is the version byte. BIP141 explains that, since a version byte is pushed before a witness program, and programs with unknown versions are considered anyone-can-spend scripts, a new script system can be introduced with a soft fork. Non-upgraded nodes do not see or validate the witness data and consider all witness programs anyone-can-spend, except the edge cases where the program is equal to 0; the BIP says wallets should always be wary of anyone-can-spend scripts and treat them with suspicion (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The activation is on the chain. The soft fork took effect at block 481,824 of the main network, which was mined on 24 August 2017, according to the heights in Bitcoin Core's chain parameters and the explorer's record of that block. The page's example is a model of the old node's view: it runs only the output script, 0 followed by 20 bytes, which leaves two items, the last of them a nonzero program, which counts as true. The library shows the same with the witness flag switched off: a witness spend with an empty witness is accepted (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (mempool.space, 2026).

The two steps of the upgrade, in the book's words, are that wallets must first create segwit-type outputs, and then those outputs can be spent by wallets that know how to construct segregated witness transactions. The new node, which does enforce the rule, handles an output of the form version and program by requiring an empty input script and checking the witness; a miner who enforces the rules never includes a block in which the witness is wrong, and so the old node, whose rules are weaker, never sees a block that the new rules reject (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

The words anyone-can-spend are exact for an old node and for a wallet that does not check. A coin held in a witness program is as safe as the number of miners that enforce the rules: if a majority did not, the witness could be ignored. This is why the soft fork was deployed with a period of signalling by miners, called version bits, which for segwit started on 15 November 2016 and had a timeout on 15 November 2017 (Lau, 2016).

nodes.example: old nodes see anyone-can-spend, new nodes check the witness
nodes.definition: Segregated witness is a soft fork: an old node sees a witness output as two pushes that anyone can spend and ignores the witness, while an upgraded node enforces the witness rules, so the two kinds of node agree on the chain as long as the miners enforce the new rules.

nodes.label: Nested segregated witness
nodes.body: A nested segregated witness output is a witness program embedded in a pay to script hash script. The book explains the case: Alice's wallet is not upgraded but Bob's is; Bob's wallet constructs a P2SH address that contains a segwit script inside it, Alice pays it without knowing anything about segwit, and Bob spends with a segwit transaction, taking advantage of the reduced cost of witness data. Both forms can be embedded: the first is noted as nested P2WPKH, the second as nested P2WSH (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A nested segregated witness output is a witness program embedded in a pay to script hash script. The book explains the case: Alice's wallet is not upgraded but Bob's is; Bob's wallet constructs a P2SH address that contains a segwit script inside it, Alice pays it without knowing anything about segwit, and Bob spends with a segwit transaction, taking advantage of the reduced cost of witness data. Both forms can be embedded: the first is noted as nested P2WPKH, the second as nested P2WSH (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The nested form solves the second scenario of the upgrade at a small price. BIP141 compares it with the native form: the output script is one byte bigger and the input script 23 bytes bigger, and it says that although a nested witness program is less efficient, its payment address is fully transparent and backward compatible for all reference clients since version 0.6.0. In the saved block 129 inputs, 95 key hash and 34 script hash, use this form (Lombrozo et al., 2015) (mempool.space, 2026).

The book gives both constructions with numbers, and the library reproduces them. For the key hash ab680255..., the redeem script is 0014 followed by the hash; its HASH160 is 3e054726...; with the version byte 5 the address is 37Lx99uaGn5avKBxiW26HjedQE3LrDCZru. For the script hash 9592d601..., the redeem script is 0020 followed by the hash, its HASH160 is 86762607... and the address is 3Dwz1MXhM6EfFoJChHCxh1jWHb8GQqRenG. The page's example computes the first address and the 23 bytes of the push of the redeem script that is the input script.

The spend runs in the order of the two mechanisms. The output script is an ordinary script hash script and the input script is a single push of the redeem script; the hash matches, and then the engine sees that the redeem script is a witness program and runs the witness rules with it. The input script must be exactly the push of the redeem script, otherwise the error is WITNESS_MALLEATED_P2SH, because anything else would let a third party change the transaction. The library runs the nested spends of a key hash and of a 2-of-3 multisignature (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Lombrozo et al., 2015).

Two hash steps are easy to confuse. The nested script hash is the legacy HASH160 of the witness program, with its version and length bytes, not of the key and not of the script; and in the nested script hash form the inner SHA-256 of the witness script is already one hash, so the data goes through the hashes of two layers. The book's two nested examples use different hashes, 9592d601... for the witness script, and a9b7b38d... for the native example, which are two different scripts and not a mistake.

nodes.definition: A nested segregated witness output is a script hash output whose redeem script is a witness program; a wallet that cannot send to a segwit address can pay the 3 address, and the receiver spends it with a witness.

nodes.label: Witness signature hash
nodes.body: The witness signature hash is the digest that a version-0 witness input signs, defined by BIP143. It is a double SHA-256 of ten items in a fixed order: the transaction version, a hash of all input outpoints, a hash of all input sequences, the outpoint of this input, the script code of the input, the value of the output spent by this input, the sequence of the input, a hash of all outputs, the lock time and the hash type. It replaced the old algorithm for witness inputs only (Lau et al., 2016).

paras.text: The witness signature hash is the digest that a version-0 witness input signs, defined by BIP143. It is a double SHA-256 of ten items in a fixed order: the transaction version, a hash of all input outpoints, a hash of all input sequences, the outpoint of this input, the script code of the input, the value of the output spent by this input, the sequence of the input, a hash of all outputs, the lock time and the hash type. It replaced the old algorithm for witness inputs only (Lau et al., 2016).

BIP143 names two weaknesses of the original algorithm. The first is that the data hashed for each signature is proportional to the size of the transaction, so the hashing grows with the square of the number of signature operations: a 1 MB block normally takes about 2 seconds to verify but a transaction of 1 MB with 5,569 signature operations could take 25 seconds. The second is that the original algorithm did not involve the amount being spent, so an offline signing device could not know the amount or the fee without the whole previous transaction (Lau et al., 2016).

The first fix is the three reusable hashes: the hash of the outpoints, of the sequences and of the outputs are computed once and reused for the other inputs, which reduces the whole process from the square to a linear amount of work. The second fix is the sixth item, the amount. The page's example is a model that follows the ten items for one input and one output and shows that changing the amount by one satoshi gives a different digest. The library's function for the same digest gives the same result for the same transaction, and the real spends of the saved block's 626 P2WPKH inputs validate with it (mempool.space, 2026).

The rules for the hash type are as before, with changes: all types commit to the amount; the removal of the signature from the script code is not applied; the single type does not commit to the input index; and for the key hash form the script code is the legacy key hash script, 0x1976a914, the 20-byte hash and 0x88ac. If the hash type does not have the anyone-can-pay flag, the hash of the outpoints is the hash of all of them, and otherwise zero; similar rules decide the hashes of the sequences and the outputs (Lau et al., 2016).

The amount is committed to by the signature, which means that a wallet signing with a wrong amount produces a signature that the network rejects: the library signs a spend with an amount one satoshi too small and the engine returns EVAL_FALSE. The model of the page is not a complete implementation, since it does not handle the other hash types or several inputs, which is what the library does and the specification defines in full.

nodes.example: sighash v0 commits to the amount of the spent output
nodes.definition: BIP143 defines the signature hash for version-0 witness programs: it hashes the parts of the transaction in a fixed order with the value of the output being spent, and it reuses three hashes for all inputs, so that the work grows with the size of the transaction and not with its square.

nodes.label: Script trees and key tweaks
nodes.body: This branch presents the three ideas that taproot, the last upgrade of the chapter, combines. The first is a tree of alternative scripts, in which only the script that is used is revealed. The second is key tweaking, in which a public key is changed by a value that commits to some data, so that paying to the changed key is also a commitment. The third is the scriptless multisignature, in which several signers make together one signature that looks like the signature of a single key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch presents the three ideas that taproot, the last upgrade of the chapter, combines. The first is a tree of alternative scripts, in which only the script that is used is revealed. The second is key tweaking, in which a public key is changed by a value that commits to some data, so that paying to the changed key is also a commitment. The third is the scriptless multisignature, in which several signers make together one signature that looks like the signature of a single key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The ideas answer the weaknesses of the script of the previous branches. A script with several paths pays for all of them in every spend, is limited in size and makes every condition public when any one is used; a multisignature script puts a key and a signature on the chain for every signer. The branch shows how a hash tree, an addition of points and a sum of signatures remove these costs, and each idea is recomputed with the library.

The reader meets the results in every taproot address. In the 6 taproot inputs of block 775,072, 5 spend with a single signature, which can be that of one person or of many, and 1 reveals a script from a tree; the data shows how a tree hides everything but the leaf that is used (mempool.space, 2026). Bitcoin Core's documentation records support for the aggregation of keys in descriptors since release 30.0 and for signing since release 31.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The first, script trees, explains the Merklized alternative script tree and why the name has two meanings. The second, key tweaks, explains pay to contract, the scriptless multisignature, and the threshold signature, which is the subject where the book's text and the BIPs differ most in strictness. The browser examples use only SHA-256 and the elliptic curve arithmetic that the page provides.

nodes.label: Trees of alternative scripts
nodes.body: This group is about committing to many scripts with one hash. A Merklized alternative script tree is a set of scripts, each complete by itself, of which only one is used; the output commits to the root of a Merkle tree over them, and a spend reveals the used script and the hashes that connect it to the root (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group is about committing to many scripts with one hash. A Merklized alternative script tree is a set of scripts, each complete by itself, of which only one is used; the output commits to the root of a Merkle tree over them, and a spend reveals the used script and the hashes that connect it to the root (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The tree takes the three costs of an IF script away: the weight, since only the executed script is in the transaction; the limit on size, since the number of scripts can grow with only one more hash for each doubling; and the loss of privacy, since the other scripts, and even their number, stay hidden. The earlier proposals BIP114 and BIP116 had the same aim, and taproot reached it by another way.

The first section describes the tree, the membership proof and the arithmetic of the commitments, with a real tree built from the hashes that taproot uses. The second section separates the two meanings of the name MAST, which the book keeps apart because one of them is wasteful. The examples run in the browser with SHA-256 alone.

The sizes the book quotes for its three-script example depend on key, signature and script sizes that the text does not give, so the page does not reproduce them; the structure of the saving, which grows with the logarithm of the number of scripts, is the part that is explained and computed.

nodes.label: Merklized alternative script tree
nodes.body: A Merklized alternative script tree, MAST for short, is the way to use a merkle tree to authorize many different spending conditions. The book describes it step by step: each member of the set of conditions is passed through a hash function to create a short commitment called a leaf; each leaf is paired with another and hashed again, giving a commitment to the leaves called a branch; the step is repeated until one identifier remains, the merkle root. A spend then carries a compact membership proof, which proves that one condition is a member without disclosing the others (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A Merklized alternative script tree, MAST for short, is the way to use a merkle tree to authorize many different spending conditions. The book describes it step by step: each member of the set of conditions is passed through a hash function to create a short commitment called a leaf; each leaf is paired with another and hashed again, giving a commitment to the leaves called a branch; the step is repeated until one identifier remains, the merkle root. A spend then carries a compact membership proof, which proves that one condition is a member without disclosing the others (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The tree removes the three drawbacks that the book finds in OP_IF scripts. Every condition adds weight and fee, because the script grows; legacy script is limited to 10,000 bytes, which allows only a few hundred branches, or about 20,000 useful branches even in a script as large as a block; and every condition becomes public when the output is spent, so that Mohammed's lawyer would see the whole script of the previous branch even when he does not sign. With the tree, only the used script is public, and the number of scripts stays hidden, from a single one to a trillion (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The cost of a tree grows slowly. The book computes it in commitments of 32 bytes: three conditions need three commitments, one of them the root; a fourth condition costs nothing more; an eighth needs one more; sixteen commitments, 512 bytes, serve over 32,000 conditions; and 128 commitments, 4,096 bytes, more than all computers could create. The page's example builds a three-leaf tree and checks two membership proofs, a long one of two hashes for the first script and a short one of one hash for the third, and rejects a proof whose hashes are in the wrong order (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The check folds the hashes upward: starting from the hash of the script, it combines the running value with each supplied hash, and compares the final value with the committed root. In the form that taproot uses, a leaf hash is a tagged hash of the leaf version and the script, a branch hash is a tagged hash of the two children sorted so that the smaller comes first, and the sorting means that a proof does not need to say whether a sibling is left or right. BIP341 gives the reason for that choice, which was suggested by one of its acknowledged contributors (Wuille et al., 2020).

The tree does not make all scripts equal. A script near the root is cheap to use and one far from it is dear, so the book restructures its example to place the most expected script in the best position, saving one commitment of 32 bytes for the common case, and notes that a Huffman tree gives the best arrangement when the probabilities are known. BIP341 adds a privacy point: the depth of a script in the tree leaks the minimum depth of the tree, which can suggest the wallet software that made it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: Two meanings of MAST
nodes.body: The name MAST has two meanings, and the book keeps them apart in a box. The earliest idea for what is now called MAST was the Merklized abstract syntax tree: in an abstract syntax tree every condition in a script creates a new branch, and such trees are widely used by compilers. A Merklized AST would commit to every part of a program. What people mostly call MAST in Bitcoin today is the Merklized alternative script tree, a backronym coined by the developer Anthony Towns (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The name MAST has two meanings, and the book keeps them apart in a box. The earliest idea for what is now called MAST was the Merklized abstract syntax tree: in an abstract syntax tree every condition in a script creates a new branch, and such trees are widely used by compilers. A Merklized AST would commit to every part of a program. What people mostly call MAST in Bitcoin today is the Merklized alternative script tree, a backronym coined by the developer Anthony Towns (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The distinction matters because it decides how much is revealed. A Merklized AST would require revealing at least one 32-byte digest for every separate part of the program, which, the book says, would not be very space efficient on the blockchain for most programs. An alternative script tree is a set of scripts, each complete by itself, of which only one is selected, so they are alternatives for each other, and it requires one 32-byte digest for each level of depth between the chosen script and the root (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

BIP114 is the 1 proposal that used the earlier name: its title is Merkelized Abstract Syntax Tree, its status is Closed, and it defines a new witness program type that uses a Merkle tree to encode mutually exclusive branches in a script. BIP116, MERKLEBRANCHVERIFY, is a Draft that proposes an opcode for proving that a data element is a member of a committed set. The book says that there were two solid proposals before an improved approach was discovered, which became taproot (Lau, 2016) (Friedenbach et al., 2017) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The cost of the alternative tree can be computed from the number of scripts. The number of 32-byte commitments is the depth of the tree plus the root: the example computes 3 for three scripts and for four, 4 for eight and 16 for 32,768, which is 96, 96, 128 and 512 bytes, the figures of the book. A balanced tree is right when all scripts are equally likely; when they are not, BIP341 advises building the tree by the known probabilities, and the book names Huffman's algorithm for it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

The book's paragraph on the cost says that with three conditions it needs three commitments and that it could also have four commitments for the same cost; the second figure must mean four conditions, which the arithmetic above confirms. There is also a limit in taproot on the depth of the tree, 128 levels, which BIP341 explains as the depth of the most space-efficient tree that could be built (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: Tweaking keys
nodes.body: This group is about changing a public key by adding to it a value that is made from other data. Pay to contract uses the tweak as a commitment to a description; the scriptless multisignature uses the sum of keys as a way to make one key from many; and the threshold signature adds the question of who signed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group is about changing a public key by adding to it a value that is made from other data. Pay to contract uses the tweak as a commitment to a description; the scriptless multisignature uses the sum of keys as a way to make one key from many; and the threshold signature adds the question of who signed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Each idea uses the same property of the curve: points can be added, and the sum of two keys is the key of the sum of the two private keys. The tweak means that a key can carry a commitment without any extra data on the chain, and the sum means that several parties can look like one. Both are what taproot builds on, since a taproot output is a tweaked key.

The first section explains pay to contract with the book's example of a podcast episode and checks that the tweaked private key matches the tweaked public key; the second shows the aggregation of keys and signatures and a signature made by three signers that verifies as an ordinary one; the third gives the arithmetic of sharing a secret so that any two of three can use it, and sets it against the n-of-n signature of BIP327.

The demonstrations of the group are teaching sketches, not secure protocols. The naive sum of keys is open to a rogue-key attack, which the standard protocol prevents with a coefficient for each key, and a threshold scheme needs more care than the secret sharing shown here. The page says so each time and cites the standard where there is one.

nodes.label: Pay to contract
nodes.body: Pay to contract, P2C, is the use of a key tweak as a commitment. The book builds on the property of elliptic curves that Alice can derive a public key from her private key and give it to Bob; Bob can add an arbitrary value to it to create a derived public key, and if he gives the value to Alice, she can add it to her private key to get the key of the derived public key. In the example, Bob buys a podcast episode from Alice, and they agree on a description, which is turned into a number by hashing it. Bob adds the number to Alice's public key and pays it. The process is called key tweaking, and the number is the tweak (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Pay to contract, P2C, is the use of a key tweak as a commitment. The book builds on the property of elliptic curves that Alice can derive a public key from her private key and give it to Bob; Bob can add an arbitrary value to it to create a derived public key, and if he gives the value to Alice, she can add it to her private key to get the key of the derived public key. In the example, Bob buys a podcast episode from Alice, and they agree on a description, which is turned into a number by hashing it. Bob adds the number to Alice's public key and pays it. The process is called key tweaking, and the number is the tweak (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The payment can later be shown to be a payment for that thing. Bob can reveal Alice's underlying key and the description, and anyone can check that the paid key equals the underlying key plus the hash commitment of the description; if Alice admits that the key is hers, she received the payment, and if she spent the funds she knew the description when she signed, as she could only sign for the tweaked key if she knew the tweak. If neither of them reveals the description, the payment looks like any other, so there is no loss of privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The book notes that because P2C is private by default we cannot know how often it is used for its original purpose, but that it is widely used today in another form, which is taproot. BIP341 describes this: the output of a taproot is a point Q computed as P plus the hash of P and m, times G, for a public key P and the root m of a Merkle tree, so that every taproot output is a pay to contract commitment to a tree of scripts, even when the tree is empty (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

The example computes the tweak as the SHA-256 of the description taken as a number modulo the curve order, adds the tweak times the generator point to Alice's public key, and checks that the point of the sum of Alice's private key and the tweak is the same point. The library does the same with the taproot tweak: the tagged hash of the key and the tree root gives the number, and the secret that signs for the output is the secret plus that number, adjusted for the parity of the point (Wuille et al., 2020).

The proof only works if the payee's underlying key is revealed together with the description, and then the payee's other uses of that key become public; fresh keys for each payment avoid this. The tweak must also be a commitment in the full sense: a hash that cannot be made to match two different descriptions. And the sum of the two is a key like any other, so an observer cannot tell a tweaked key from an ordinary one, which is both the privacy of the scheme and the reason why the proof must be given on purpose.

nodes.example: pay to the key P + t*G, where t is a hash of the contract
nodes.definition: Pay to contract is a key tweak that commits to an agreed description: the payer adds the hash of the description, as a number, to the public key of the payee, and the payee spends with the private key plus the same number.

    m = (3 * a[0] * a[0] * pow(2 * a[1], -1, P) if a == b else (b[1] - a[1]) * pow(b[0] - a[0], -1, P)) % P
    x = (m * m - a[0] - b[0]) % P
    return x, (m * (a[0] - x) - a[1]) % P

nodes.label: Scriptless multisignature
nodes.body: A scriptless multisignature is the other way to require cooperation from several keys. The book distinguishes script multisignatures, which use the OP_CHECKSIG-style opcodes, from scriptless ones. Each participant creates a secret like a private key, called a partial private key, and derives a partial public key from it; the partial public keys are shared and combined into the scriptless multisignature public key. To spend, each participant makes a partial signature, and the partial signatures are combined into a regular full signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A scriptless multisignature is the other way to require cooperation from several keys. The book distinguishes script multisignatures, which use the OP_CHECKSIG-style opcodes, from scriptless ones. Each participant creates a secret like a private key, called a partial private key, and derives a partial public key from it; the partial public keys are shared and combined into the scriptless multisignature public key. To spend, each participant makes a partial signature, and the partial signatures are combined into a regular full signature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The result is smaller and more private. The combined key looks the same as any other Bitcoin public key, and the combined signature looks the same as any other signature, so a third party cannot tell whether a signature was made by one person or by a million people. For scripted multisignatures the number of bytes grows with every key and signature, and the number of keys is disclosed; for scriptless ones the size is constant. The book names two costs: the known secure algorithms need more rounds of interaction or more careful management of state, which is hard for nearly stateless hardware signing devices, and a threshold signature does not reveal who signed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

BIP327 standardizes the scheme, MuSig2, for BIP340 keys and signatures: signers create one aggregate public key and cooperatively create ordinary Schnorr signatures valid under it, in two communication rounds, and signing requires all signers. The on-chain footprint is essentially a single public key and one signature, which BIP327 says is more compact and has lower verification cost than a key and a signature for each signer with the counting opcode of tapscript, and the number of signers is not limited by any consensus rule (Nick et al., 2022).

The sum of keys is the base of the scheme: the point of the sum of private keys is the sum of the points of the private keys, which the example checks for three participants. A signature is added in the same way, if the participants add their random nonces too: each makes a partial signature from its nonce, key and a common challenge, and the sum of the partial signatures is a signature that the standard verification accepts. The library does this for two, three and five signers, each time producing 64 bytes that verify under the sum of the keys (Wuille et al., 2020).

The simple sum is not secure. A participant who sees the others' keys before choosing its own can choose a key that cancels theirs and so control the combined key alone; the standard prevents this by multiplying each key by a coefficient that depends on all the keys, and by nonces of two points. The library's sketch is labelled as a sketch for that reason. The standard is also an n-of-n scheme and not a threshold scheme, as BIP327 says in its motivation (Nick et al., 2022).

nodes.example: many partial keys and signatures sum to one key and one signature
nodes.definition: A scriptless multisignature is a way for several participants to produce one public key and one signature that look exactly like those of a single signer; the script that would count the keys and signatures disappears.

nodes.label: Threshold signature
nodes.body: A threshold signature is the t-of-k version of the scriptless multisignature. The book explains the difference with a script: in scripted threshold signing, Alice, Bob and Carol agree that any two of them signing is enough, and if Alice and Bob sign, their signatures are on the chain and prove to anyone who knows their keys that they signed and Carol did not. In scriptless threshold signing a signature from Alice and Bob cannot be told from one by Alice and Carol or by Bob and Carol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A threshold signature is the t-of-k version of the scriptless multisignature. The book explains the difference with a script: in scripted threshold signing, Alice, Bob and Carol agree that any two of them signing is enough, and if Alice and Bob sign, their signatures are on the chain and prove to anyone who knows their keys that they signed and Carol did not. In scriptless threshold signing a signature from Alice and Bob cannot be told from one by Alice and Carol or by Bob and Carol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

That property is a benefit and a cost at the same time. It is beneficial for privacy, since the chain says nothing about who took part; but even if Carol claims that she did not sign, she cannot prove it, which the book says may be bad for accountability and auditability. The book's conclusion for many users and uses is that the reduced size and increased privacy outweigh the occasional difficulties of creating and auditing these signatures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mathematics of sharing a secret is old and simple, and the page shows its smallest case: a secret is the constant term of a line, the three shares are the values of the line at the points 1, 2 and 3, and any two shares determine the line and therefore the secret, by Lagrange interpolation at zero. The example checks all three pairs. A threshold signature scheme applies this idea to a signing key so that the key itself is never assembled in one place, which this page does not demonstrate.

The reader should not confuse the sketch with a protocol. BIP327, the standard that the chapter cites, is n-of-n and not a t-of-n threshold scheme, as its own motivation states; so there is no deployed standard of the course's sources for the threshold case. What the library shows is the part that is pure arithmetic: shares of 12345 at 1, 2 and 3 reconstruct it from any two, and one share alone gives no information about the secret, since for every possible secret there is a line through that share (Nick et al., 2022).

The book names the second cost directly: scriptless threshold signing does not reveal who signed. A business that needs an audit trail has to keep it outside the chain, or use a script multisignature, in which the signatures are the audit trail. The first cost, interaction, matters most for a signing device in a safe deposit box, which with a scripted multisignature is visited once and with a scriptless one possibly two or three times (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
