nodes.label: Taproot and tapscript
nodes.body: This branch presents the last upgrade of the chapter. Taproot is a new kind of output, a witness program of version 1, that can be spent in two ways: with one signature made for its key, or by revealing one script out of a tree of scripts that the key commits to. Tapscript is the slightly different version of the script language that the revealed scripts use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch presents the last upgrade of the chapter. Taproot is a new kind of output, a witness program of version 1, that can be spent in two ways: with one signature made for its key, or by revealing one script out of a tree of scripts that the key commits to. Tapscript is the slightly different version of the script language that the revealed scripts use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The upgrade combines the ideas of the previous branch. A tree of alternative scripts gives many conditions for the price of one hash; a tweaked key makes the same output a commitment to the tree; and a scriptless multisignature lets the parties who agree spend with a single signature that no one can tell from the signature of a single person. The book's reason is that a contract whose outcome is predictable should be settled by mutual satisfaction, and then nothing about its other conditions needs to be on the chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The data shows the result. Of the 6 taproot inputs in the first 599 transactions of block 775,072, 5 are spent by the key path with one signature, and the 1 script path spend reveals a script of 720 bytes with a control block of 33 bytes (mempool.space, 2026). Taproot became active at block 709,632 on 14 November 2021, and Bitcoin Core's source records the activation height in a comment on the warning height that is one miner confirmation window later (mempool.space, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The first, taproot outputs, explains the output, the spending by the key path, the spending by the script path and the control block that proves the script belongs to the output. The second, tapscript, explains what changes in the script language, the counting opcode that replaces the old multisignature opcode, and the opcodes that make a script succeed. Every example is a real transaction signed and verified by the chapter's library.

nodes.label: Taproot outputs
nodes.body: This group is about the output itself and the two ways to spend it. The output holds a public key and nothing else, and it can be spent either by the key or by a script that the key commits to. The group explains the output, the key path, the script path and the control block (Wuille et al., 2020).

paras.text: This group is about the output itself and the two ways to spend it. The output holds a public key and nothing else, and it can be spent either by the key or by a script that the key commits to. The group explains the output, the key path, the script path and the control block (Wuille et al., 2020).

A single kind of output replaces the separate pay to public key and pay to script hash outputs. BIP341 states the aim: all outputs become spendable by either a key or, optionally, a script, and they are indistinguishable from each other, so that as long as the key path is used it is not revealed whether a script path was also permitted (Wuille et al., 2020).

The first section computes the output key from an internal key and a script tree. The second spends it with a signature, and the third spends it with a script and a proof. The fourth section explains the control block, the string of bytes that connects the revealed script to the output. The examples sign real transactions and verify them with the library, and the browser examples recompute the keys and the signature check with SHA-256 and curve arithmetic alone.

The group describes the rules of the consensus and the practice of wallets. BIP341 is the consensus text; BIP86 only says how a single-key wallet should derive its keys; and the choice of an internal key for a contract is advice and not a rule. Where the page gives advice, it names the document it comes from.

nodes.label: Taproot output
nodes.body: Taproot is the name of the output type and of the soft fork that added it. The book builds it from the earlier ideas: pay to contract tweaks a key to commit to an agreement, and taproot commits instead to the program code of a contract by tweaking with the root of a MAST. The key that is tweaked is a regular public key, so it can require one signature, the signatures of several people, or even be made so that no signature for it can exist. The tweaked key is the taproot output key, and the key before the tweak is the taproot internal key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Taproot is the name of the output type and of the soft fork that added it. The book builds it from the earlier ideas: pay to contract tweaks a key to commit to an agreement, and taproot commits instead to the program code of a contract by tweaking with the root of a MAST. The key that is tweaked is a regular public key, so it can require one signature, the signatures of several people, or even be made so that no signature for it can exist. The tweaked key is the taproot output key, and the key before the tweak is the taproot internal key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The construction gives two ways to satisfy the same contract. If everyone interested agrees, they can sign with the key and nothing else appears on the chain. If they do not, one of the scripts is revealed. The book notes that a spend by a million participants of a very complex contract and a spend by one user of his own coins then look the same on the chain. The only downside the book knows is that a contract that wants a tree but no cooperative clause must still put an internal key, about 33 bytes, on the chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

BIP341 gives the formula and says what the program is: a witness version 1 whose programs consist of 32-byte encodings of points Q, with Q computed as P plus the hash of P and m times G, for a public key P and the root m of a Merkle tree whose leaves consist of a version number and a script. Bitcoin Core's constants name the same sizes: the program has 32 bytes, the leaf version for tapscript is 0xc0 and the mask that leaves the version is 0xfe (Wuille et al., 2020) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The example takes the generator point as the internal key and a tree of one leaf that holds the script OP_TRUE, whose leaf hash is a85b2107...; the output key is 9b6ce0db... with an even y coordinate, and a different tree gives a different key.

The example follows the formula. The leaf hash is the tagged hash of the leaf version and the script; with a single leaf it is the root. The tweak is the tagged hash of the internal key and the root, taken as a number; the output key is the internal point plus the tweak times the generator, and only its x coordinate is the program. The library computes the same value and the same address form, and BIP341's wallet test vectors, seven in all, give the same keys, addresses and control blocks, as the verification script reports (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A tree is not required. If the spending conditions do not need a script path, BIP341 and BIP86 both advise tweaking with an empty tree, Q = P plus the tagged hash of P alone, times G, so that the key commits to an unspendable script path instead of having no script path at all; the reason, which BIP341 gives, is that a key made from several keys can otherwise be given a hidden script path by a dishonest participant. When no key should be able to spend, the advice is a point with unknown discrete logarithm; the example in BIP341 is the hash of the generator point's encoding (Wuille et al., 2020) (Chow, 2021).

nodes.example: the output key is the internal key plus a tweak that commits to the tree
nodes.definition: A taproot output is a witness program of version 1 whose program is the 32-byte x coordinate of a point Q, computed as the internal key P plus the tagged hash of P and the root of a script tree, times the generator point; paying to Q is also a commitment to the scripts.

nodes.label: Key path spending
nodes.body: Key path spending is the spending of a taproot output with a signature for its key. The book describes it as the case in which spending is possible using just the key, such as a single signature or a scriptless multisignature, and says that the data put on the chain is the public key in the witness program and the signature on the witness stack. In BIP341's rules, if exactly one element remains in the witness stack after the optional annex is removed, the key path is used, and that element is interpreted as a signature that must be valid for the output key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

paras.text: Key path spending is the spending of a taproot output with a signature for its key. The book describes it as the case in which spending is possible using just the key, such as a single signature or a scriptless multisignature, and says that the data put on the chain is the public key in the witness program and the signature on the witness stack. In BIP341's rules, if exactly one element remains in the witness stack after the optional annex is removed, the key path is used, and that element is interpreted as a signature that must be valid for the output key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

The key path is the cheap and private way, and BIP341 says that ideally outputs are spent with it, because it prevents observers from learning the spending conditions of a coin. A key path spend can be a normal payment from a wallet with one key or several, or the cooperative settlement of a hidden contract. The signature is made with the secret key that matches the output key, which for a tweaked key is the internal secret key plus the tweak, adjusted for the parity of the point (Wuille et al., 2020).

Alice's payment to Bob's cafe in chapter 6, in block 775,072, spends a taproot output this way: its witness has one element of 65 bytes, a Schnorr signature of 64 bytes followed by the hash type byte 01, and the library accepts it against the output it spends (mempool.space, 2026). In a signature made with the default hash type, the type byte is left out and the element is 64 bytes. Spending an output of the same kind with a script tree costs the same, since the signature does not depend on the tree except through the tweak: a transaction with one such input weighs 308 weight units in the library's example, whether the output committed to a tree of three scripts or to none (Wuille et al., 2020).

The example checks a BIP340 signature in the browser. The output key was computed from the internal secret key 7 with an empty tree, the message is a stand-in for the signature hash of a transaction, and the signature was made with the tweaked secret key; the check holds, and it fails for another message. If the signature were made with the untweaked internal key, the real library rejects it with the error SCHNORR_SIG; the tweak is part of the secret (Wuille et al., 2020).

The signature commits to more than the outputs, and the format of the signature has a trap. BIP341 builds the signed message from the hash type, the version, the lock time, and, unless the flag ANYONECANPAY is set, from the amounts and the scriptPubKeys of all the outputs being spent; it also commits to the spend type, which holds the annex flag. A signature of 64 bytes means the default hash type, and a signature of 65 bytes must not end in the byte 00, because that would let anyone, even a miner, turn a 64-byte signature into a 65-byte one and change the wtxid and the fee rate of the transaction; the library rejects such a signature with SCHNORR_SIG_HASHTYPE (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.example: the witness is one 64-byte signature for the output key
nodes.definition: Spending a taproot output by the key path needs one witness element, a BIP340 signature for the output key; it is checked like any other signature and shows nothing about any script the output might have committed to.

nodes.label: Script path spending
nodes.body: Script path spending is the spending of a taproot output by one of its scripts. The book lists what the witness holds: a version number; the underlying key, the taproot internal key; the script to execute, called the leaf script; one 32-byte hash for each junction in the Merkle tree along the path that connects the leaf to the root; and any data needed to satisfy the script, such as signatures or preimages (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Script path spending is the spending of a taproot output by one of its scripts. The book lists what the witness holds: a version number; the underlying key, the taproot internal key; the script to execute, called the leaf script; one 32-byte hash for each junction in the Merkle tree along the path that connects the leaf to the root; and any data needed to satisfy the script, such as signatures or preimages (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reason for the design is to reveal as little as possible and to pay only for what is used. The script path is for the case in which the key path is not applicable, for instance because the parties failed to reach agreement; BIP341 says that such a spend leaks that there is a script path and that the key path was not applicable, so the other leaves stay hidden but the existence of the tree does not. The cost grows with the depth of the leaf, 32 bytes for each level (Wuille et al., 2020).

In block 775,072 the 1 script path spend is an inscription: its tapscript begins with a 32-byte key and OP_CHECKSIG, then OP_FALSE OP_IF and an envelope of data, which the OP_IF never runs, with the content type image/png near the start; the witness has three elements, a signature of 64 bytes, a script of 720 bytes and a control block of 33 bytes, so the tree has one leaf (mempool.space, 2026). The example of the page builds a tree of three scripts and shows that the proof of the first script has two hashes and that of the third has one, and that either folds up to the root the output key committed to. In the library, a spend of a leaf of a three-leaf tree with two signatures is accepted, and the same spend with the wrong parity bit in the control block is rejected as WITNESS_PROGRAM_MISMATCH (Wuille et al., 2020).

The verifier works in a fixed order, which BIP341 specifies. It removes the annex if there is one; with at least two elements left, it takes the last element as the control block and the one before it as the script; it computes the leaf hash from the leaf version and the script, folds in each hash of the control block, takes the result as the root, and checks that the tweaked internal key equals the output key, including the parity bit. Only then does it run the script, with the rules of its leaf version, on the items that remain (Wuille et al., 2020).

A script path spend gives up something the key path keeps. It shows that the output had a tree and which leaf was used, and the depth of the leaf leaks the minimum depth of the tree. An inscription is not a different kind of spend; it uses the script path, with a script that contains data that is never run, and nothing in the rules limits the data except the size of the witness and the rules of the standard relay policy (Wuille et al., 2020) (mempool.space, 2026).

nodes.example: the witness shows a script, a proof and the data that satisfies it
nodes.definition: Spending a taproot output by the script path reveals one script of the committed tree, the control block that connects the script to the output key, and the items that satisfy the script; no other script of the tree is shown.

nodes.label: Control block
nodes.body: The control block is the proof that the revealed script belongs to the output. The book mentions it only in a note that it should be introduced; BIP341 defines it as the last stack element of a script path spend, of length 33 plus 32 times m, for a value of m that is an integer between 0 and 128, inclusive. Its first byte is the leaf version with the parity of the output key's y coordinate in its lowest bit, the next 32 bytes are the internal key, and the rest are the sibling hashes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

paras.text: The control block is the proof that the revealed script belongs to the output. The book mentions it only in a note that it should be introduced; BIP341 defines it as the last stack element of a script path spend, of length 33 plus 32 times m, for a value of m that is an integer between 0 and 128, inclusive. Its first byte is the leaf version with the parity of the output key's y coordinate in its lowest bit, the next 32 bytes are the internal key, and the rest are the sibling hashes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

Each field has a use. The parity bit lets the verifier lift the x coordinate of the output key to a single point, which, BIP341 says, is not strictly needed to check the commitment but is needed to allow batch verification. The leaf version lets later soft forks define new script rules for other versions while tapscript uses 0xc0. The sibling hashes are sorted before they are hashed, so the control block does not need to say whether each sibling is on the left or the right (Wuille et al., 2020).

Bitcoin Core names the sizes: the base size of the control block is 33, each node is 32 bytes and the largest number of nodes is 128, so the largest control block is 33 plus 32 times 128, or 4,129 bytes. The one script path in the block has a control block of 33 bytes, whose first byte is 0xc1, leaf version 0xc0 with the parity bit set, and whose 32-byte internal key is 00fd948e...; it has no sibling hash because the tree has one leaf. In the example of the page's library, the control block of the first leaf of a tree of three scripts is 97 bytes, the 33 plus two hashes (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (mempool.space, 2026).

The example takes the control block apart: the first byte masked with 0xfe gives the leaf version 192, which is 0xc0, and masked with 1 gives the parity 1; the internal key is the 32 bytes after it; and the number of sibling hashes is the length less 33, divided by 32, which is 0 here. A control block whose length is not 33 plus a multiple of 32, or is outside 33 to 4,129 bytes, is rejected with the error TAPROOT_WRONG_CONTROL_SIZE (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille et al., 2020).

The limit of 128 levels is not a practical one. BIP341 explains that the most space-efficient tree can be built by the Huffman algorithm, with branch lengths about the base-2 logarithm of the inverse of the probability, and that a branch longer than 128 would hold a script with a chance of use below 1 in 2 to the power 128, which is the security bound, so such a script could probably be removed. A tree with that many leaves could not be written down anyway (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.label: Tapscript
nodes.body: This group is about the version of the script language that the leaves of a taproot tree use. The leaf version 0xc0 selects it, and BIP342 defines it. It keeps most of the language of the earlier sections and changes how signatures are checked, how many signatures are counted and what happens with opcodes that the old language did not use (Wuille et al., 2020).

paras.text: This group is about the version of the script language that the leaves of a taproot tree use. The leaf version 0xc0 selects it, and BIP342 defines it. It keeps most of the language of the earlier sections and changes how signatures are checked, how many signatures are counted and what happens with opcodes that the old language did not use (Wuille et al., 2020).

The changes have two aims. The first is to allow the batch verification of Schnorr signatures, which the old multisignature opcode makes impossible; the second is to make the language easier to extend with soft forks. BIP342 summarises both: the inefficient CHECKMULTISIG opcodes are disabled, a new opcode creates the same policies in a batch-verifiable way, MINIMALIF removes a malleability vector, and the OP_SUCCESS opcodes allow new opcodes more cleanly than the OP_NOP opcodes (Wuille et al., 2020).

The first section lists the changes and runs each one through the library, in a real script path spend. The second explains the opcode that counts signatures and shows the m-of-n multisignature rewritten with it, including the sizes in bytes. The third explains the opcodes that make a script succeed at once and the rule that allows them to be redefined later.

BIP342 changes more than the book mentions: it also adds a budget for the signature operations of each script, a rule that unknown key types succeed, and a rule that the annex is committed to by the signature. The page names these where they matter and gives the document for the rest.

nodes.label: Changes in tapscript
nodes.body: The book lists the major differences. The old OP_CHECKMULTISIG and OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY are removed and the new OP_CHECKSIGADD takes their place. All signature operations use the Schnorr algorithm of BIP340. A signature check that is not expected to succeed must be fed OP_FALSE, also called OP_0, instead of a signature, and anything else fed to a failed check makes the entire script fail. Opcodes that were unusable become OP_SUCCESS opcodes, which make a script succeed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The book lists the major differences. The old OP_CHECKMULTISIG and OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY are removed and the new OP_CHECKSIGADD takes their place. All signature operations use the Schnorr algorithm of BIP340. A signature check that is not expected to succeed must be fed OP_FALSE, also called OP_0, instead of a signature, and anything else fed to a failed check makes the entire script fail. Opcodes that were unusable become OP_SUCCESS opcodes, which make a script succeed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The empty-signature rule is what makes batch verification possible. A verifier that checks many Schnorr signatures together needs to know that every non-empty signature must be valid, so that it can add them to the batch and not run each one to learn the result of the check. In the old language, a failed check could leave an invalid signature on the stack without harm; in tapscript an invalid, non-empty signature fails the whole script, and an empty one only makes the check return false (Wuille et al., 2020).

BIP342 states the other changes. The disabled opcodes fail when they are executed and are ignored in a branch that is not executed, as OP_RETURN does, and the reason given is to make sure that people who keep using OP_CHECKMULTISIG notice a problem at once and not later. The MINIMALIF rule, which is only a policy rule in P2WSH, becomes a consensus rule: the argument of OP_IF and OP_NOTIF must be exactly empty or exactly the one byte 01, to make scripts that take branch information from the stack easier to make non-malleable. In the library, a leaf with OP_CHECKMULTISIG is rejected with TAPSCRIPT_CHECKMULTISIG, an OP_IF fed the byte 02 with TAPSCRIPT_MINIMALIF, and a lone check fed the byte 01 as its signature with SCHNORR_SIG_SIZE, while an empty signature gives the plain EVAL_FALSE (Wuille et al., 2020).

The example compares the sizes of the same policy: the legacy script for 2 of 3 is 105 bytes and the tapscript form is 104 bytes, because each key costs 34 bytes in both forms, a push of 33 bytes in the legacy script and a push of 32 bytes followed by one signature opcode in the tapscript, and the legacy form needs one more byte, the count of keys, which the tapscript form does not write because the opcodes count the keys themselves. The signature rules are checked with real signatures in a leaf with one key: the right signature is accepted, a signature of another key is rejected as SCHNORR_SIG, an empty signature makes the script fail without an error in the signature, and a signature of the wrong length is rejected for its size (Wuille et al., 2020).

There is an extra rule for upgrades, which the book leaves out. A public key in tapscript that is not 32 bytes long is of an unknown type, and any non-empty signature for it is accepted without being checked, which makes it possible to define new key types or signature algorithms by a soft fork; Bitcoin Core's relay policy therefore refuses such scripts, so that they are not relayed before a meaning has been given to them. The same is true of an unknown leaf version, whose scripts are accepted by consensus and discouraged by policy (Wuille et al., 2020) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.definition: Tapscript disables the old multisignature opcodes, makes every signature check use BIP340 Schnorr signatures, requires a signature that is not expected to succeed to be the empty value, and makes the MINIMALIF rule part of the consensus.

nodes.label: OP_CHECKSIGADD
nodes.body: OP_CHECKSIGADD is the opcode that replaces OP_CHECKMULTISIG. The book says that it increments a counter by one when it successfully verifies a signature, which makes it possible to count how many signatures passed and compare the count with the number wanted. BIP342 gives the equivalence: it is functionally the same as OP_ROT OP_SWAP OP_CHECKSIG OP_ADD, but takes one byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

paras.text: OP_CHECKSIGADD is the opcode that replaces OP_CHECKMULTISIG. The book says that it increments a counter by one when it successfully verifies a signature, which makes it possible to count how many signatures passed and compare the count with the number wanted. BIP342 gives the equivalence: it is functionally the same as OP_ROT OP_SWAP OP_CHECKSIG OP_ADD, but takes one byte (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2020).

The multisignature opcode could not be kept because it does not combine with batch verification: it tries signatures against keys in order until enough match, so a verifier cannot tell which pairs are meant to be valid. Here every signature is tied to its key by position, and the empty value says explicitly that a key does not sign. BIP342 gives the translation: a script of m, n keys, n and CHECKMULTISIG, with witness 0 and m signatures, becomes the first key and CHECKSIG, each of the other keys with CHECKSIGADD, and m NUMEQUAL, with a witness of one element for each key that is either its signature or empty (Wuille et al., 2020).

The library runs the translation. A 2-of-3 leaf of 104 bytes, with the keys of Mohammed, Saeed and Zahra, is spent in a real taproot transaction with the witness empty, signature, signature, and the interpreter accepts it; with one signature only it fails with EVAL_FALSE, since the count is 1, and with a non-empty garbage value in the place of an absent signature it fails with the error SCHNORR_SIG_SIZE. Mohammed's three-path contract of the previous branch, rebuilt as three tapscript leaves, weighs 577, 617 and 414 weight units for its three paths, against 585, 584 and 509 for the 192-byte P2WSH script, and a key path spend of the same output would weigh 308, so the script paths save weight only for the rarest path and the key path is the real saving (Wuille et al., 2020).

The example is a model of the opcode, not the interpreter: the signature is valid when it is in a set, empty when it is the empty value, and anything else stops the script. It accepts two signatures and an empty value in any of the three places; it refuses a count of one and a count of three, since the final comparison is for equality, NUMEQUAL, and not for at least two. The witness is listed in the reverse order of the keys, because the last element is used first (Wuille et al., 2020).

There are costs. A signature check that fails for a reason other than being empty fails the script, so a script that wants to test a signature and continue must use the empty value. Each non-empty signature counts against the budget of the script: BIP342 sets the budget at 50 plus the serialized size of the input's witness, and each non-empty signature takes 50 from it. A 2-of-3 spend with a witness of 335 bytes has a budget of 385, which allows 7 signatures, so an honest script is far from the limit (Wuille et al., 2020).

nodes.example: each valid signature adds one; an empty signature adds nothing
nodes.definition: OP_CHECKSIGADD pops a public key, a number and a signature, adds one to the number if the signature is valid, leaves it unchanged if the signature is empty and fails the script if the signature is not empty and not valid; a multisignature is a chain of these followed by a comparison.

nodes.label: OP_SUCCESS opcodes
nodes.body: The OP_SUCCESS opcodes are opcode values that make a tapscript valid as soon as it is read. The book explains the idea: opcodes of previous versions that were unusable are redefined so that using them makes the entire script succeed, which lets a future soft fork redefine them as not succeeding under certain circumstances; that is a restriction and so possible by soft fork, whereas defining a non-succeeding operation as a success could only be done by a hard fork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The OP_SUCCESS opcodes are opcode values that make a tapscript valid as soon as it is read. The book explains the idea: opcodes of previous versions that were unusable are redefined so that using them makes the entire script succeed, which lets a future soft fork redefine them as not succeeding under certain circumstances; that is a restriction and so possible by soft fork, whereas defining a non-succeeding operation as a success could only be done by a hard fork (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The old route for new opcodes was OP_NOP, which can only look at the stack and leave it alone. An OP_SUCCESS opcode can be given more power. BIP342 gives the reasons: it may write to the stack, it may lift the limit on the size of stack elements because it comes before the check of the initial stack, it may change the behaviour of existing opcodes so that they work with it, and since it makes even a script that cannot be decoded succeed, it can be used to introduce multi-byte opcodes or a whole new language (Wuille et al., 2020).

BIP342 lists the numbers: 80, 98, 126 to 129, 131 to 134, 137 and 138, 141 and 142, 149 to 153, and 187 to 254, which are 87 values, and the same list is in Bitcoin Core's IsOpSuccess function. The library runs a real script path spend of a leaf made of the single opcode 0xbb, which is OP_SUCCESS187, with an empty witness besides the script and control block, and the interpreter accepts it; a leaf that begins with 0x50 followed by bytes that do not decode is accepted too, and Bitcoin Core's policy flag that discourages the opcodes makes the same spend fail with DISCOURAGE_OP_SUCCESS (Wuille et al., 2020) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The model in the example scans the opcodes in order and succeeds at the first one in the list; it does not run the rest, which is the point. The real scan decodes the script first and fails if a script is cut short before any such opcode was found, so a truncated push before an OP_SUCCESS fails, while one after it does not. A wallet must never put such an opcode in a script by accident: anyone could spend the output, since the script succeeds without any signature (Wuille et al., 2020).

The same property is a danger for the one who writes a script. A leaf with an OP_SUCCESS opcode is valid without a signature, so an output whose only leaf is such a script is an output that anyone can spend. Relay policy refuses these scripts for that reason, and also so that wallets and nodes can notice the mistake before any funds are lost. The names are renamed in the code as OP_SUCCESS80 to OP_SUCCESS254 (Wuille et al., 2020) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: 87 opcode values make a tapscript succeed at once
nodes.definition: In tapscript, 87 opcode values that were unused or disabled are renamed OP_SUCCESSx, and a script in which one is found succeeds unconditionally even when the bytes after it could not be decoded; a later soft fork can give any of them a meaning, as that can only turn a valid script into an invalid one.

io.code:
(lambda g: (exec("success = {80, 98, *range(126, 130), *range(131, 135), 137, 138, 141, 142, *range(149, 154), *range(187, 255)}   # the numbers BIP342 lists
def tapscript_result(opcodes):                           # a model: scan the opcodes in order
    return 'success' if any(o in success for o in opcodes) else 'run the script'
result = (len(success), tapscript_result([0x51, 0xac]), tapscript_result([0x51, 187, 0xff]))", g), g['result'])[1])({})

findings: Background

Chapter 7 explains how a Bitcoin output asks for authorization and how a spender authenticates. It presents the script language and the stack on which it runs, the input and output scripts and their separate execution, pay to public key hash, scripted multisignatures and the oddity of OP_CHECKMULTISIG, pay to script hash, data recording with OP_RETURN, absolute and relative timelocks, flow control and a three-path example, segregated witness in its native and nested forms, and the three ideas that taproot combines - a Merklized tree of scripts, pay to contract and scriptless multisignatures - followed by taproot and tapscript.
Comparative analysis

The statements of the chapter were checked by running them. A Bitcoin Script interpreter written with the Python standard library, faithful to the interpreter of Bitcoin Core at the pinned commit, accepts all 1,237 script tests of Core's script_tests.json, reproduces all 500 legacy signature hashes of sighash.json and the 7 signature hash and key path vectors of BIP341's wallet vectors, accepts all 1,022 inputs of the first 599 non-coinbase transactions of block 775,072 under today's consensus rules and under every policy flag it implements, rejects each tampered input, and reproduces the BIP340 test vectors. Every worked example of the chapter's page is a program that runs on this interpreter or on the standard library alone.
Comparative analysis

The first 599 non-coinbase transactions of block 775,072 hold 1,022 inputs and 1,668 outputs. By input type: P2WPKH 626, P2PKH 194, P2SH-wrapped P2WPKH 95, P2WSH 57 (all multisignatures), P2SH-wrapped P2WSH 34, P2SH multisignatures 10, taproot key path 5 and taproot script path 1; by output type: P2WPKH 754, P2SH 490, P2PKH 314, P2WSH 69, P2TR 33 and data outputs 8. Segregated witness inputs are 812 of 1,022, about 79 percent. None of the 91 witness scripts contains a timelock or conditional opcode; the one tapscript is an inscription that begins OP_FALSE OP_IF.
Comparative analysis

The chapter states the lock time rule as an equal-or-higher comparison. Bitcoin Core's IsFinalTx tests whether the lock time is less than the block height (or the median time past), so a transaction with lock time N is first final in block N plus one; the difference is one block and changes no conclusion, but an example that sets a lock time to the next block's height is off by one under the source.
Comparative analysis

The chapter gives three months as 12,960 blocks or 7,760,000 seconds. Twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty blocks of ten minutes are exactly 90 days, and 90 days are 7,776,000 seconds; the second figure is 16,000 seconds short. The error does not affect the opcode.
Comparative analysis

The chapter says that BIP68 and BIP112 were activated in May 2016. The BIPs record that the voting period started on 1 May 2016, and Bitcoin Core's chainparams puts the first block under the rules at height 419,328, which the explorer dates 4 July 2016.
Comparative analysis

The chapter describes OP_CHECKMULTISIG as comparing the signatures with the keys starting from the first key listed. Bitcoin Core's interpreter starts from the key at the top of the stack, which is the last key listed; the signatures are matched in the same order and the worst case, as many checks as keys for a one-signature spend, is the same.
Comparative analysis

The chapter says that the spend of its three-script tree uses 383 bytes against 412 bytes without the tree, saving 29. The sizes of the keys, signatures and scripts of the figure are not given, so the figures cannot be derived; the saving of the structure is computed instead, one 32-byte commitment for each doubling of the number of scripts. The same paragraph says that four commitments would cost the same as three; the arithmetic supports four conditions, not four commitments.
Comparative analysis

The standards' figures reproduce with the interpreter: a 2-of-3 multisignature script of 105 bytes against 104 bytes as a tapscript with OP_CHECKSIGADD; the largest control block of 33 plus 32 times 128 bytes; 87 OP_SUCCESS opcode values in BIP342 and in Bitcoin Core's IsOpSuccess; the taproot activation block 709,632 on 14 November 2021 with a warning height of 711,648 one confirmation window later; and, for the contract of the chapter's three-path example rebuilt as a taproot tree, spending weights of 577, 617 and 414 weight units by script path and 308 by key path, against 585, 584 and 509 for the P2WSH script.
Conclusion

For the course, the chapter's lesson is that authorization is a program, and that each upgrade of Bitcoin's scripts is a way of making the program cheaper to show and harder to see: a hash instead of a script, a witness instead of an input script, a tree instead of a list, and at the end a single signature that stands for any of them. The second lesson is that the scripts run in the same way on every node because the language is stateless and bounded, and that every figure of the chapter can be checked by running it.
Contemporary developments

Several policy details have moved since the chapter was written. The default budget for OP_RETURN data in Bitcoin Core is now 100,000 vbytes shared by all the data outputs of a transaction, a figure the chapter does not quote; the relay policy no longer requires the redeem script of a P2SH output to be standard and caps its signature operations at 15; and Bitcoin Core's descriptors accept key aggregation with musig() from release 30.0 and signing from release 31.0, so the scriptless multisignatures the chapter describes as future work have a standard (BIP327) and an implementation.
Contemporary developments

Two stories of the chapter come from sources that are not the book. The OP_RETURN bug of 28 July 2010 (CVE-2010-5141) is recorded by the Bitcoin Wiki and is visible in the difference between the sources of Bitcoin 0.3.0 and 0.3.7; the fork of 4 July 2015 after the activation of BIP66 is recorded by the network alert of that day, which names the 950-of-1,000 threshold, a fork of 6 blocks and about half of the hash rate mining without validating.
Terms used without definition

An audit of the explanations written for this chapter listed every technical term they use and compared it with the concepts of chapters 1 to 6 and of this chapter. The terms used without a concept of their own were the stack and its execution, the truth of a script, the public key hash, the DER encoding, the dummy element, the count of signature checks, the redeem script, the witness program and the sigops of a script hash. Each was added as a concept of this chapter, so that no term in the document is used before it is explained.

stories.title: The script that ended with a true result
stories.who: Satoshi Nakamoto, the author of the software; the people who found two bugs and showed them on the test network
stories.where: the Bitcoin test network, in the first release line of the software (0.3.x); the lesson is carved into every later script engine
stories.story: On 28 July 2010 two bugs were discovered and demonstrated on the test network. One of them, recorded as CVE-2010-5141, let an attacker spend coins that they did not own: the first software joined the input script and the output script into one program and treated OP_RETURN as a jump to the end, so an input script of 1 followed by OP_RETURN ended the run with a true value and the output script never ran. The bug was never exploited on the main network and was fixed in version 0.3.5, and by version 0.3.7 the two scripts run one after the other and OP_RETURN fails. After the discovery many unused script words were disabled for safety, and the chapter's library shows that today's tapscript turns disabled values such as OP_LSHIFT, number 152, into OP_SUCCESS opcodes, which make a script succeed on purpose.
stories.lesson: Run the two scripts separately, and fail closed on anything unknown
stories.source: The Bitcoin Wiki entry on Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, saved in ch07-evidence: CVE-2010-5141, 2010-07-28, wxBitcoin and bitcoind, 'OP_RETURN could be used to spend any output', fixed in 0.3.5, never exploited on the main network; the sources of Bitcoin 0.3.0 and 0.3.7 (script.cpp), whose difference the chapter's library reproduces; BIP342 on OP_SUCCESS opcodes; the book's chapter 7 section on separate execution. stories.title: Half the miners did not check the block
stories.who: the miners who enforced BIP66 and the roughly half of the hash rate that mined without validating; the Bitcoin Core developers who wrote the alert
stories.where: the Bitcoin network from block 363,725; the mining pools whose software built on an unchecked block
stories.story: BIP66 made strict DER the only valid encoding of a signature, and it took effect once 950 of the last 1,000 blocks were version 3, which happened early on 4 July 2015, at block 363,725. A small miner that had not upgraded then produced an invalid block, as was expected, but roughly half of the network's hash rate was mining without fully validating blocks and built on top of it, so a fork of 6 blocks lasted from 02:10 to 03:50 UTC and a second of 3 blocks followed on 5 July. No double spend was seen in the first fork; several large miners lost income, and the alert advised users of lightweight wallets to wait 30 more confirmations. Bitcoin Core 0.9.5 and later were unaffected because they checked the rule.
stories.lesson: A rule that you do not check for yourself protects nobody
stories.source: The Bitcoin.org network alert 'Some Miners Generating Invalid Blocks', 4 July 2015, last updated 15 July 2015, saved in ch07-evidence: the 950-of-1,000 threshold, the roughly 50 percent of hash rate that was SPV mining, the forks of 6 blocks (4 July, 02:10 to 03:50 UTC) and 3 blocks (5 July), no double spend in the first, the 30 extra confirmations; BIP66 and Bitcoin Core's chainparams for the activation height 363,725 (block timestamp 01:54:32 UTC, mempool.space). Photo: a bitcoin mining farm, 14 June 2014 - Marko Ahtisaari, CC BY 2.0; it is a general view of mining hardware and not of the 2015 pools.

stories.title: From a patented signature to one key for a million people
stories.who: Claus-Peter Schnorr, who invented the signature scheme; Pieter Wuille, Jonas Nick, Tim Ruffing and Anthony Towns, the authors of BIPs 340, 341 and 342
stories.where: block 709,632, mined on 14 November 2021, the block at which the taproot rules took effect
stories.story: Claus Schnorr patented the signature algorithm he discovered and kept it out of open standards and open-source software for almost two decades, so cryptographers of the early 1990s built the DSA family that led to the ECDSA signatures Bitcoin used from its first release. BIP340 was assigned in January 2020 to standardise Schnorr signatures on Bitcoin's curve, BIP341 and BIP342 added the taproot output and tapscript, and the rules took effect at block 709,632 on 14 November 2021, a block of 2,043 transactions. Bitcoin Core's source still notes the height, with a warning height one miner confirmation window later at 711,648. A payment such as Alice's in the chapter spends such an output with one 64-byte signature, which looks the same whether one person or a million made it.
stories.lesson: Patents delayed Schnorr for decades; a soft fork brought it to every wallet
stories.source: The book's chapter 8, section 'ECDSA Signatures' (the patent, 'almost two decades', ECDSA the only signature algorithm until the taproot soft fork in 2021); BIP340 (assigned 2020-01-19, 64-byte Schnorr signatures); BIP341 and BIP342; Bitcoin Core src/kernel/chainparams.cpp at commit 05bc2f5, 'taproot activation height + miner confirmation window'; the block record from mempool.space: height 709,632, timestamp 2021-11-14 05:15:27 UTC, 2,043 transactions.
